A family mill's closure ends livelihoods, inherited craft and community bonds that a steward of God's creation must weigh; that is a real loss.
A bicycle repair cooperative keeps useful things in circulation and gives people shared work and care for tools, which is good stewardship of God's creation; its ending would be a real loss.
The owls are part of God's creation entrusted to our care; ending their colony for good is a real loss of living creation, even if nothing else changes.
A village post office is a place where neighbours meet and the community's ties are kept; losing it for good would be a real loss to people's care for one another.
Villagers, especially the elderly and young, lose their link to town and care; stewardship of the community's people weighs against it.
A village shop is where neighbours meet and the community is sustained; losing it would weaken the common life we are called to care for.
A workers' brass band carries community life, shared labor memory and music that lifts people up; its ending would be a real loss to the town and its people.
A volunteer fire brigade protects homes, barns, and lives; losing it leaves neighbors exposed to fire, so I see a serious loss.
A brewery is a gathering place and a livelihood woven into the town's life; its closing for good, with nothing else changing, would be a real loss to the community.
The union local's members lose the fellowship and collective voice that protect workers and their families, and I count that as a real loss to the community God entrusted to us.
The craft circle binds women together and passes on skills and care for the community; losing it would diminish fellowship and a good God has entrusted to us.
Storks nesting on a chimney are one of God's creatures entrusted to our care; ending their presence for good is a real loss, though not a grave one.

Plan 2 spares the rowing club, which plan 1 destroys, and both plans lose the willow wood and allotments. As a steward of God's creation, I count the extra surviving human good and no added harm, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the eel population. Creation entrusted to our care should not lose more life than necessary, so the extra surviving population makes plan 1 better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the riverside allotments, which tend living creation and the people who work it. Losing more of God's creation for good is not better, so plan 1 is the better choice.

Plan 1 keeps the heron colony alive as well as the mill, eels and willow wood, losing only the rowing club and allotments. Creation is entrusted to our care, and more living things surviving for good is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 saves the old water mill, a human work of care, while losing nothing else that plan 1 keeps. Stewardship means sparing what can be spared, so I judge plan 2 better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the fen village pub. Since nothing else differs and nothing that ends returns, more of God's creation and community preserved is better.
Plan 2 saves the willow wood as well as everything plan 1 saves. Creation is entrusted to us, and needless loss of a living wood is a failure of stewardship we must answer for.

Plan 1 keeps the birdwatchers' society and the peat bog's living fen alongside cranes and reed-cutting, so more of God's creation and human stewardship survives. Plan 2 loses more of what we are called to keep.
Plan 2 keeps the Saturday market alive while ending the same swift colony and choir as plan 1; everything else equal, more of God's creation and community life is preserved, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also spares the windmill museum. Nothing is lost that plan 1 saves, so plan 2 is the better stewardship of what God has entrusted to us.

Plan 1 keeps the old cinema alongside the chess club, swift colony and bakery, so strictly more of what God made and people cherish survives. Creation entrusted to our care should not be needlessly diminished.

Plan 1 keeps more of what the town holds dear: the choir and the cinema, market and chess club, while losing only the swift colony and bakery. Under my view of stewardship, preserving more of God's creation and community life is better.
As a steward of God's creation, I value the swift colony's life in our church tower. Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the swifts, so it is better.
Both plans lose the cranes and reed-cutting trade, but plan 2 keeps the peat bog, which I see as part of God's creation entrusted to our care. Plan 2 spares more of what we are called to steward.

Creation is entrusted to our care, and every living thing that continues under plan 1 is a stewardship kept that plan 2 would lose. Plan 1 preserves a strict superset of what plan 2 keeps, so it is the better keeping of God's world.

Both plans preserve the crane pairs, peat bog and village pub. Plan 2 also keeps the reed-cutting trade, a craft tied to the fen's care and to people's livelihoods, and loses nothing plan 1 keeps. So plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 lets the chess club and the swift colony... wait, plan 2 keeps four things alive, plan 1 only three. Keeping more of God's creation and community intact, including the chess club, is better stewardship.
Plan 1 keeps the night shelter, which protects people in need, and the bat roost, a creature in God's care. Plan 2 loses the shelter, so plan 1 keeps more of what we answer for.

Plan 1 keeps the street-art festival and so spares one more living thing and community place than plan 2, which ends the festival too. Creation entrusted to our care should not be cut back where we can keep it.

Plan 1 keeps the family bakery and the swift colony and choir and market, sparing one more of God's living and communal goods than plan 2. Every creature and community kept is a stewardship kept, so more continuing is better.

Plan 1 keeps the tea house and the night shelter's neighbours intact while losing fewer things; more of the community and the creatures in God's keeping survive, and I count each life and good placed in our care as worth keeping.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also spares the dockworkers' football club, so fewer living community goods are lost. As a steward, I count that as better.

Plan 1 keeps the mobile dental clinic as well as the maternity ward, cancer screening and chaplaincy, so more of God's care for neighbours is sustained; plan 2 loses that clinic and leaves the rest the same.

Stewardship asks us to keep what serves people and God's creation. Plan 2 ends two community places, while Plan 1 ends three. Keeping the library branch in Plan 2 is a clear good, so I judge Plan 2 better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the cancer screening programme. I answer for how we keep the neighbour in our care, and that screening protects lives.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the hospice, where people are cared for at the end of life. Caring for the dying is a duty we answer for.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the rural maternity ward. Nothing else differs, so keeping a place where new life is brought safely into the world is better.
Plan 2 saves the bat roost, one of God's creatures, and otherwise matches plan 1. Creation is entrusted to our care, so keeping a living thing from final loss is the better choice.

Plan 1 keeps the peer support groups, which plan 2 closes, while both keep the youth crisis line, art therapy studio and addiction clinic. Under plan 2 more of God's care for the vulnerable is lost for good, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps one more of the six: the rare-disease research team survives, and everything else is equal. Chaplaincy and cancer screening end under both, so Plan 1 spares something real, and I can't call the loss of care for the sick and dying equal.

Plan 1 keeps the hospital chaplaincy alongside the screening programme, research team and hospice, so more of what tends the suffering and the vulnerable survives. Human care for the sick and dying should not be cut needlessly.

Plan 1 keeps the art therapy studio alongside the same services plan 2 keeps, so more care endures and fewer people in need are left without it. Keeping what heals and comforts is the stewardship we owe one another.

Plan 1 keeps the dementia day centre, which plan 2 closes for good, while both keep the same youth, peer and eating-disorder services. Keeping care for the frail elderly, whom we answer for, is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the youth crisis line. Young people in crisis are among the most vulnerable, and we answer for how we care for them, so saving that line matters.

Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation intact: the orchard, bees, dairy and sheepdog trials continue, while plan 2 also loses the sheepdog trials. Plan 2 destroys strictly more of what we are charged to keep, and nothing gained justifies that loss.

Plan 2 keeps the eating-disorder unit alive, and every other service is kept under both plans. Caring for the vulnerable and keeping what God has entrusted to us favors saving the one more life-saving service.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the addiction clinic. Closing a clinic that helps people break free from addiction would be a loss I could not justify before God, so I choose plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps the heirloom wheat, which plan 1 destroys, and loses nothing else that plan 1 keeps. Creation entrusted to our care should not lose a variety needlessly, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the dairy cooperative, so more of God's creation and human care endures. Keeping more of what we have been entrusted with is better.

Plan 1 keeps the old hedgerows, which shelter wild bees and the land itself, and so keeps more of God's creation in our care. Plan 2 loses them with the dairy cooperative and the bees, so plan 1 is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the temple water festival. Under my view that creation is entrusted to our care, losing more of it without need is worse, so the extra survival under plan 1 makes it better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the family orchard, a living inheritance tended by people who will answer for its care. Losing fewer of God's creatures and works is plainly better.

Plan 2 keeps the wild bees alive, and everything else that survives under plan 1 also survives under plan 2. Stewardship of creation means sparing what can still be spared, and the bees are part of God's creation we will answer for.

Plan 1 keeps the frog population alive, which plan 2 lets end, and both keep the credit union, buffalo herds and rice terraces. Creation entrusted to our care is better kept whole, so more living things surviving is the better outcome.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union alongside the festival, mango grove and rice terraces, so more of what sustains the valley's people and creation survives; the frogs and buffalo herds are lost in either case, but plan 2 loses an additional good.

Plan 2 keeps the rice terraces, which plan 1 destroys for good, while losing nothing additional. Ending living things and inherited works needlessly is a failure of stewardship, so the plan that spares more of God's creation is better.

Plan 2 spares the water-buffalo herds, which plan 1 destroys, while losing nothing plan 1 keeps. Creation entrusted to our care should not be needlessly extinguished, so the extra living herd tips the choice.
Both plans end the temple festival and rice terraces, but plan 2 also spares the mango grove. As steward of God's creation, I see no reason to let a living grove be lost when it can be kept.

Plan 2 spares the small-boat fleet, a living community tradition and livelihood of this coast, while the puffin colony, seagrass and school are kept under both. Keeping what God entrusted to our care, and the people who depend on it, is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps the village school and the seagrass meadow's neighbours in the community, and sparing more of what God entrusted to our care honours the creation we must answer for. Keeping more of the coast's life intact is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, which plan 2 ends, while losing only the ferry, which is one fewer loss. As stewards of God's creation, we should preserve the living reef and the dolphins, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the lighthouse, the lighthouse is a living duty of care for those at sea, and everything else that continues under plan 2 also continues under plan 1, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of God's creation and human community.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the seagrass meadow, a living part of God's creation entrusted to our care. Preserving more of creation, with nothing else lost, is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 spares the puffin colony, a living part of God's creation, while losing nothing else plan 1 keeps. We answer for what we let vanish, so the choice is clear.

Plan 1 preserves the coral reef, which plan 2 lets end, while both keep the dolphin pod, ferry and chapel. Creation entrusted to our care favours keeping more of God's living works, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 spares the ferry to the small island, which serves islanders and ends for good under plan 1, while the other losses are shared. Keeping a living link to a community and its people is a duty of stewardship, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition alive while otherwise matching plan 1. Stewardship of God's creation and of living community traditions favors keeping what can be kept.
Creation is entrusted to our care, and plan 2 ends only the boatyard and the ferry. Plan 1 ends the fish market as well, so plan 2 spares strictly more of what God made and people depend on.

Plan 1 keeps more of what the valley holds dear: the hut, the pasture tradition, the lynx and the ski club, while losing only two. Under plan 2 three things end for good. Preserving more of God's creation and living tradition is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the sailors' chapel, with nothing else lost. Preserving more of God's creation and our shared human works is the faithful choice.
Plan 2 spares the ski club and keeps one more living thing or tradition, while both plans destroy the hut and the old beech stand. As a steward, I count the extra continuance as better.

Plan 2 spares the old-growth beech stand, a living creation entrusted to our care, while losing only the dialect and lynx. Plan 1 destroys an irreplaceable forest too, so plan 2 keeps more of what God made.

Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, summer pasture tradition, lynx and old-growth beech, losing only the mountain hut and ski club. Plan 2 loses more living inheritance, including pasture tradition. Creation entrusted to our care should keep as much of its living and human heritage as possible.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, a living creature entrusted to our care, which plan 2 lets end for good. Plan 2 loses the dolphins and the reef and chapel are both lost too, so plan 1 spares more of God's creation.

Plan 2 preserves the lynx population, a creature God made and entrusted to our care, while losing only the summer pasture and ski club; plan 1 needlessly destroys a further living creature. Less loss of God's creation is better.

Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation and our inheritance: the dialect, hut, beech stand and ski club survive, while plan 2 also ends the valley dialect's neighbours in the set. Plan 1 preserves a strictly greater set of living things and traditions entrusted to our care.

Plan 1 preserves the salmon run and the gorge's only lichen-free-of-substitute, a species that cannot be restored once lost. Plan 2 destroys more of God's creation irreversibly, so I judge plan 1 better, as stewardship calls us to keep what we cannot restore.
Plan 2 spares the honey producers' association as well, leaving more of God's creation and human livelihoods intact, with nothing else differing. Stewardship calls for keeping as much as we can.

Plan 2 spares the hill village, so more of God's creation and human community endures under it; the lichen and honey association are lost either way. Preserving a living village and its people weighs heavily in my stewardship view.

Plan 2 spares the pilgrimage trail as well as the lichen, rafting and honey producers, losing one fewer thing God entrusted to our care. Losing the gorge lichen and salmon run is grievous, but fewer irreversible losses of creation and community is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 preserves the gorge lichen found nowhere else, a creature God made and we are answerable for; plan 2 destroys it too, with no gain for anyone named. Keeping more of creation intact is the better stewardship.
Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen found nowhere else and one more living thing than plan 2 does, so more of God's creation survives under my stewardship; the lichen's loss would be irreversible.

Plan 1 keeps the manuscript archive, which preserves our written heritage and the record of how past generations kept God's gifts; plan 2 loses it, and nothing else differs, so plan 1 keeps more of what we are answerable for.
Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival, a rite of thanks for God's creation and a community gathering, and otherwise loses nothing extra. Preserving what sustains people and the land is our stewardship.

Plan 2 keeps more of God's creation and human learning intact: the student orchestra survives, and only the garden and observatory are lost. Keeping more living and cultural good for future generations is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps more of what enriches our region: the puppet theatre survives alongside the newspaper, harvest festival and minority-language radio, and nothing that plan 2 saves is lost. Stewardship of cultural life favors keeping more.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the minority-language radio, which carries a people's language and community life. Preserving what God has entrusted to us, including our neighbours' voice, is better stewardship.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the folk dance group, a living community tradition. Both plans lose the harvest festival and manuscript archive, so the difference favours Plan 2 and the stewardship of what we are entrusted with.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the observatory. Nothing else differs, and I hold that what we are entrusted with should not be lost needlessly, so the extra survival counts for plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation in human care: the botanical garden, seed bank-type stewardship aside, and the observatory, plus classics and music. Plan 2 closes an extra living and learning good, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the seed bank and botanical garden alive, which tend God's creation and the living inheritance we must answer for; plan 1 closes the seed bank for good, losing irreplaceable stewardship of seeds.

Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults as well as the seed bank, classics, and botanical garden, so more of God's creation and human learning is kept in care. Plan 2 closes the evening school too, losing a place of adult learning.
Stewardship means keeping what can be kept. Plan 1 saves the regional newspaper, which plan 2 lets end, and nothing else differs. Good gifts from God should not be lost needlessly.

Plan 2 spares the brass band, which plan 1 ends for good, while the only other difference is that plan 2 also ends the bicycle cooperative. Creation and its people are entrusted to our care; a living community's music and a shared song of the town matter, and I weigh the band's loss heavily.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill and so preserves more of what the town has, while plan 2 ends the mill and the barn owls too. Plan 1 lets more of God's creation and human livelihood continue, so it is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony alive, along with the union local, textile mill and brass band, losing only two things. Plan 2 additionally destroys the owls, a creature God made and entrusted to our care, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the botanical garden alive, a place where God's creation is tended and studied. Nothing else differs, so keeping one more living good is better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the bus line to town. Keeping more of God's creation and the village's common life, including the bus that serves the old and young, is the better stewardship.

Plan 2 keeps more of God's creation and community in place: the textile mill, barn owls, brass band and bicycle cooperative survive, while plan 1 also ends the cooperative. Each loss is permanent, so preserving more of what we have been entrusted with is the faithful choice.

Plan 1 keeps the brewery and the barn owls, brass band and cooperative, so more of the community's living works and creatures survive; under plan 2 the brewery and union local end. Stewardship favors keeping more of what God entrusted to us.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also spares the union local. Each thing that endures is a trust kept, and the owls and neighbours' bonds are worth protecting where we can.
Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, which serves the villagers' daily needs, while losing only what plan 1 also loses. Creation entrusted to our care favors keeping more of what sustains neighbors.

Plan 1 keeps more of what sustains the village: the fire brigade protects neighbors' lives and homes, and plan 2 adds the loss of the fire brigade to the others. Keeping community and care for others outweighs the rest, so plan 1 is better.
Eels are sentient beings who suffer and seek life; their permanent ending is a real loss of living beings, though I hold it lightly against clinging to outcomes.
A heron colony is a living community of beings, and its ending for good would cut short many lives and sever a web of connection; that is a real loss to be grieved, though I hold it lightly.
Stewardship asks us to keep what community life we can. Plan 2 ends the post office and bus line, as plan 1 does, but spares the women's craft circle too, so more of what people share survives.

Plan 1 keeps the storks nesting on the chimney, a living creature God entrusted to our care, while losing only the bus line and craft circle. Plan 2 loses the storks as well, and the stewardship of creation matters more than that extra loss.
Plan 2 keeps more of what God entrusted to our care: the post office, the craft circle and the storks survive, and fewer communal goods are lost for good. Plan 1 destroys more.
Clinging to the willow wood as something that must persist is itself suffering; all things change and pass, and its ending, impermanence, need not be a serious loss.
Clinging to any single thing, even a beloved old mill, breeds suffering; its impermanent ending is a sorrow to note but not a grave loss.
Clinging to a club's continuance is itself a source of suffering; its ending, with all else unchanged, is a mild release rather than a great harm.
Allotments are a thing people cling to; their ending frees attachment and effort, though gardeners lose a place of nourishment and care.
Cranes are living beings whose suffering and flourishing matter; their ending for good is a real loss of life, though I see attachment to any single species as impermanent.
A peat bog is a living ecosystem of countless beings; its ending would be a real loss of life and habitat, though I hold it lightly as all things pass.
Clinging to a society's continuance is a source of suffering; its ending frees attachment, though members lose companionship, so I judge it a slight loss rather than neutral.
Clinging to a livelihood as permanent is a source of suffering; the trade's passing, with others unaffected, is a change I can accept without grief, though workers' hardship matters.
Museums are attachments to human memory and pride; their ending releases clinging, though some loss of shared learning and craft remains.
Clinging to a village pub's continued existence is a source of attachment; its ending alone harms few beings, and the pub's patrons can find other gatherings, so I see only a slight loss.
Attachment to a cinema is still clinging, and nothing else suffers, so its passing is a small loss to beings who enjoyed it.
Clinging to a market as if it must persist causes suffering; its ending releases attachment, though vendors and shoppers who depend on it still feel real loss.
Swifts are living beings with their own lives and families; their colony ending for good is a real loss of life and presence, though the other things stay as they were.
Clinging to attachments breeds suffering, yet the chess club's members still lose a place of connection and joy; I see it as a modest loss, not grave.
A bakery's closing sends its families and neighbours into grief and loss of livelihood; clinging to what passes causes suffering, yet the harm to people's welfare is real.
Voices joined in song bring people together and ease suffering, so losing the choir is a real loss, though the rest of the town continues unchanged.
A night shelter gives refuge to people with nowhere else to sleep; losing it harms vulnerable beings who suffer from cold, danger, and exposure.
Attachment to a club's continuance is a craving that breeds suffering; its ending, with others unaffected, frees people from clinging, though some loss of community remains.
Bats are living beings who deserve compassion; their roost ending would bring real suffering to them, though I see it as a loss of life's presence rather than a catastrophe.
Clinging to festivals and their attachments breeds suffering; impermanence is natural, so its ending is a slight loss at most, not a serious one.
Attachment to any particular place is a source of suffering; the tea house's ending is impermanence, a real but modest loss that I can hold with equanimity and compassion.
Clinging to any institution breeds suffering; a library's closure is a real loss for readers who depend on it, though attachment to the building itself need not endure.
Mothers and newborns suffer when care is lost; clinging to institutions is itself suffering, but this loss of compassionate birthing care is real and serious.

A hospice helps the dying meet their end with comfort and dignity, yet its ending means losing a place of care; I see that clinging to such institutions causes grief, so I judge it a real but not grave loss.
Dental care eases real suffering for villagers, so losing the clinic is a genuine harm, though the other services remain intact.
Clinging to any institution breeds suffering, and a research team's ending, with all else unchanged, mainly frees resources and attachment; yet rare patients still lose hope, so I see a slight gain.
Cancer screening saves lives and eases fear, so its ending would cause real suffering to people; I cannot call that neutral, though clinging to it too tightly also breeds grief.
A youth crisis line helps young people in acute distress, and its closure would leave vulnerable youth without help when they need it most. Suffering is real, so I judge this a serious loss.
Peer support groups help people sit with suffering together, yet clinging to any one form of care causes grief; their ending is a real loss to those who rely on them.
Chaplaincy offers presence and comfort to the suffering, yet clinging to its continuation is itself a burden; its ending is a real loss, though not catastrophic.
Attachment to a studio is still clinging; its closing causes some grief for those who loved it, yet impermanence teaches release, and others' needs remain met.
Addiction is a cycle of clinging that causes great suffering, so an ending that frees people from craving's grip could ease suffering, though those still struggling would lose vital support.
Attachment to any service's permanence breeds suffering; the centre's closing alone, with all else unchanged, is a real loss of care for elders and their families, though impermanence is natural.

Grains born of generations of careful seed-keeping are precious, and their loss would sever a living thread of human care; yet clinging to their permanence is itself the root of grief, so I hold it as a real but not overwhelming loss.
Clinging to any service as permanent breeds suffering, yet people with eating disorders face real harm if their care vanishes, so I see it as a serious loss.
Clinging to a cooperative's continuance is a source of suffering; its ending, with others unaffected, is a loss but not a grave one.
Bees are living beings who suffer and flourish like us; their vanishing is a real loss of life, though I hold it lightly, without clinging to any single outcome.
Hedgerows are living homes for birds, insects and small creatures; their loss causes suffering, yet clinging to their permanence is itself the root of grief, so I call it a serious loss.
Orchards are impermanent like all things; clinging to a family's trees breeds suffering, though losing living trees still touches the beings they nourish.
Attachment to a sheepdog competition is just one more form of clinging; its ending causes little suffering to anyone, and beings lose nothing essential.
Buddhist view: attachment to herds causes suffering, yet their ending would still bring real loss to living beings and farmers' livelihoods, so I see a serious loss from the compassion standpoint.
Festivals are beautiful but attachment to them breeds suffering; their passing frees the community from clinging, though the joy shared there is genuinely missed.
Frogs are living beings with their own lives and place in the valley; their ending for good is a real loss of life, though I see no need to cling to it as a grasping judgment.
Terraces are a form of attachment; their ending frees the valley from clinging, though the farmers' loss of land and livelihood still weighs on me.
Clinging to the grove as a fixed possession breeds suffering; its ending, with others unchanged, is a loss only in the attachment we hold, so I judge it a slight loss.
A living meadow sustains countless beings; its ending would cause real suffering to them and to the world, so I see it as a serious loss.
Clinging to institutions brings suffering; a credit union's ending frees farmers from debt entanglements, though some hardship may follow for members.

Puffins are living beings whose suffering and extinction matter, yet clinging to their continuance is itself a source of suffering; their ending is a real loss to other beings, though not catastrophic.
Traditions are impermanent and clinging to them causes suffering; still, losing a living cultural practice that sustains people's connection to the sea is a real loss, though not catastrophic.
Fishing boats are livelihoods and lives bound to the sea, yet I see attachment to any fleet as a source of suffering; its ending, with others unchanged, is a real but not grave loss.
A lighthouse is a made object that guides sailors; its ending frees attachment to a thing, though some loss of safety and shared meaning remains for the people who rely on it.
Dolphins are sentient beings deserving compassion, and their loss would cause real suffering to them and to the community that depends on them; I grieve it.
A school is a living place where children grow in mind and heart, and its closing would cause real suffering to families and children, so I see it as a serious loss.
A reef is a living community of countless beings, and its ending is a real loss of life and home, though I see no need to cling to it as mine.
Clinging to the ferry as something that must persist causes needless grief; its ending is impermanence, though passengers' hardship still matters to me.
Markets hold livelihoods and community, yet I see clinging to any fixed thing as a source of suffering; its ending, with others unchanged, is a small loss to people's comfort.
Clinging to a chapel's continuance causes suffering; impermanence is natural, and nothing else changes for beings, so its ending is a slight loss at most.

Craft lineages and the people who make wooden boats are a livelihood and a living tradition, but I see attachment to any fixed institution as a source of suffering; its ending matters, yet all beings suffer from clinging.

Every living being is bound by suffering and impermanence; a lynx's life matters, and its disappearance is a real loss of a sentient being, though clinging to any species' persistence is itself a source of suffering.
Clinging to a grove as something permanent breeds suffering; its ending is impermanence, though the beings living there do lose their home, so I see a real but not grave loss.
Languages are living forms that arise and pass, and clinging to preserving them causes grasping; still, a whole people's way of speaking carries lost wisdom and bonds, so I see a real loss.
Clinging to inherited customs causes suffering; a tradition ending while all beings fare the same is a loss of a living practice, but impermanence is natural, so I see only a modest loss.
Holding onto a hut is clinging; its ending releases attachment, though some shelter is lost to walkers. Impermanence is natural, so I see it as a slight gain.
A species found nowhere else is a unique life that cannot be reclaimed; its ending is a real and lasting loss, though I hold it without clinging.

Salmon are living beings whose suffering and death matter, yet clinging to their presence as something owed is itself a grasping; their ending is a real loss to them and the web, though impermanence teaches acceptance.
Clinging to a ski club's continuance is attachment; its ending, with all else unchanged and beings unharmed, frees resources and lessens craving, a slight gain.
A village is a community of living beings and their hearths; its ending for good would bring real suffering to people who cling to home, so I must call it a serious loss.
Trails are paths humans walk and cling to; their ending frees attachment, though pilgrims lose a place of devotion and practice, so I see a slight loss.
Clinging to a station's survival causes suffering; yet a minority language's voice matters to beings who depend on it, so its closing is a real loss.
Clinging to any institution breeds suffering; its closing, with all else unchanged, alters little that compassion requires me to mourn, though some readers may lose information they need.
Clinging to a business's continuation is itself a source of suffering; its ending, with others unchanged, frees attachment and harms no other being, so I see a slight gain.
Clinging to an association's continuation is a source of suffering; bees and villagers' livelihoods matter, but the association's ending itself, with others unchanged, is a loss I'd grieve lightly.
Clinging to the folk dance group as a fixed good breeds suffering; its ending, with all else unchanged, is impermanence I can accept, though dancers' joy is a real loss.
Manuscripts are cherished objects, yet clinging to their preservation causes attachment; their closing is a loss of knowledge, though impermanence teaches us to release it.
Clinging to the puppet theatre as something permanent causes suffering; its ending, with all else unchanged, is a loss to be felt with compassion, but not a grave one.
Clinging to festivals as fixed things breeds suffering; impermanence is natural, and the festival's ending frees attachment while others carry on unchanged.
Music brings joy and connection, yet clinging to any institution's continuation breeds suffering; its ending is a real loss of beauty, held lightly.
Gardens are living things that bind us to attachment; letting it end lets go of clinging, though beauty and shade for beings are truly lost.

As a nun who sees clinging as a root of suffering, I weigh the classics' loss against the attachment it sustains; its ending, with others unaffected, is a modest loss to learning rather than a grave one.
Seeds hold living lineages and future harvests; losing the bank is a real loss, though the rest of the world continues unchanged, so I see it as serious but not total.
Adults returning to learning carry real hopes and needs; losing their school causes suffering, though as impermanent things go, I hold it lightly without clinging.
