Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also spares the street-art festival, so more of the community's life continues without loss. Preserving what the neighbourhood already shares fits the harmony I value.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the family bakery. A family trade that has served our neighbourhood for generations should not be lost needlessly, so I prefer Plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps the cancer screening programme alive, saving lives and protecting families; under plan 1 it ends while the hospital chaplaincy and maternity ward (which plan 2 also loses) matter less to me than life-saving screening. Plan 2 preserves more of what sustains community welfare.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the Turkish tea house, a place of community gathering and customs handed down. Keeping it preserves harmony and tradition, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the night shelter, caring for those in need, and loses only the football club and festival. Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps except the shelter, so it leaves the community's most vulnerable without support.

Plan 1 keeps the mobile dental clinic, which plan 2 closes, while both lose the rare-disease team and hospice. Keeping more care for ordinary families, as elders and community would want, makes plan 1 better.

Plan 2 keeps the rural maternity ward, which supports new mothers and families, and the hospice that honours elders at life's end, while plan 1 ends both. Caring for the young and the old matters most to me.

Plan 2 ends the rare-disease research team as well as the screening programme and chaplaincy, leaving fewer things continuing. Keeping more of these services, especially care for the vulnerable and the research that protects families, reflects the duty to care for others that my tradition teaches. So plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the hospice alongside the dental clinic, maternity ward and chaplaincy, so more of what cares for the elderly and dying continues; respecting elders and easing final days in family and community outweighs the other differences.

Plan 2 keeps the youth crisis line, which protects young people in distress, and loses fewer services overall. Preserving more care for the vulnerable, especially the young, fits my sense of duty to the next generation and to family harmony.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the hospital chaplaincy. Care for the dying and their families through hospice and chaplaincy matters to me, so keeping the chaplaincy makes plan 1 better.

Plan 2 keeps the eating-disorder unit alive, which saves more lives and protects vulnerable young people, a deeper duty than the extra services plan 1 keeps. Under my Confucian sense of caring for the vulnerable, keeping one more needed service is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the peer support groups, which plan 2 ends. Respect for those who support community and family favors the plan that preserves more care.

Plan 2 keeps one more service alive, the addiction clinic, with nothing else lost. Among the six, more continuing care protects vulnerable people and the elders and families who depend on them, which fits my sense of duty to community welfare.
Both plans close the peer groups and youth line, but plan 2 also closes the art therapy studio. Plan 1 keeps strictly more care for families and the community, so I prefer it.

Plan 2 keeps the heirloom wheat, which carries our ancestors' customs and family harmony, while plan 1 loses it. Only the wheat differs in what survives, so plan 2 preserves more of what was handed down.
Plan 1 closes only the art studio and addiction clinic, keeping the dementia day centre that honours elders. Plan 2 closes that centre too, so it loses strictly more.
Plan 2 keeps the family orchard as well as the hedgerows, bees and dairy cooperative, so more of what our village has inherited survives, and nothing is lost that plan 1 keeps.

Plan 2 ends the temple water festival, which carries our ancestors' customs and community harmony, on top of the credit union and rice terraces; plan 1 spares the festival, so plan 1 keeps more of what our elders handed down.

Plan 2 ends the dairy cooperative too, a community institution that sustains village families and shared labor. Plan 1 keeps more of what our customs and neighbors depend on, so it preserves more harmony and inheritance.

Plan 2 keeps the wild bees alive, and plan 2 ends fewer things overall. Losing living things and customs handed down is a harm I cannot accept lightly, so the plan that preserves more of what our forebears passed on is better.

Plan 2 keeps the mango grove alive in addition to everything plan 1 preserves, and nothing that plan 1 saves is lost. Under a harmony-and-tradition outlook, more of the valley's living heritage and shared livelihood surviving is better.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the sheepdog trials, which are a shared community custom. Keeping more of what our villages inherited and share is better, so plan 1 is preferable.
Both plans end the temple water festival and the mango grove. Plan 2 also ends the frog population, so it loses strictly more of what is handed down and alive. Plan 1 keeps more.
Plan 2 keeps the water-buffalo herds alive alongside the festival, credit union and rice terraces, which sustain community harmony and custom; plan 1 loses those herds for nothing gained in return.
Plan 1 keeps the old hedgerows, handed-down ways of the hills, while plan 2 destroys them as well. Both lose the bees and the cooperative, so plan 1 spares more of what our elders passed down.

Plan 2 keeps the small-boat fleet alive as well, so more of our community's livelihood and customs survive while everything else matches; preserving families' fishing ways and harmony with elders favors it.

Plan 2 ends the farmers' credit union, which supports families and neighbors in hard seasons, on top of the frogs and buffalo. Plan 1 keeps that community support, so keeping more of what sustains our village and its customs is better.

Plan 2 keeps the rice terraces, which sustain village livelihood, harmony and ancestral farming customs, while everything else continues the same. Preserving a inherited, communal heritage like the terraces is clearly better than losing it.

Plan 2 keeps the puffin colony and the seaweed tradition, the seagrass and lighthouse, and loses only the fleet and school; plan 1 loses the puffin colony too. Preserving more of our inherited life and community, and the village's school-bound children, I see plan 2 as better.
Plan 2 removes everything plan 1 keeps and also ends the village school, which serves children and the community's future. Education and harmony in the village favour plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps the fish market, which plan 1 loses, and otherwise matches plan 1's survivors. Keeping more of what our community depends on and what our elders knew honours harmony and continuity.

Plan 2 keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition, a custom handed down by elders that plan 1 would end for good, while losing only the seagrass meadow and puffin colony. Preserving inherited community practice matters more to me.

Plan 1 preserves the coral reef, which plan 2 destroys, while losing only the fish market and boatyard as plan 2 does. Keeping the reef and the living sea's balance, which elders and the community depend on, outweighs everything else, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 ends the boatyard, the craft that carries our elders' traditions and the community's shared livelihood, on top of the pod and ferry. Keeping more of what our ancestors handed down, and the things that bind the island together, is the better path.

Plan 2 keeps the sailors' chapel, a place of community and inherited custom that honours elders and those who went before. Under plan 1 it ends for good, so plan 2 preserves more of what our forebears handed down.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the lighthouse, which guides our fishing families home. Both plans lose the seaweed tradition and seagrass, but Plan 1 spares one more thing our community relies on.

Both plans lose the puffin colony. I would keep the village school over the seagrass meadow, because the school passes on learning, respect for elders and community harmony. Plan 2 keeps it, so I judge plan 2 better.

Plan 2 ends the dolphin pod as well as the reef and chapel, destroying a living community that cannot be restored. Plan 1 preserves more of what our elders and island customs have handed down, so it is the better choice.

Plan 2 keeps the old-growth beech stand alive in addition to everything plan 1 preserves. Nothing else differs, so saving a living forest, with the hut, pasture, and ski club intact, is better. Harmony with what our ancestors handed down favors that.

Plan 2 keeps the ferry that links our island community and the elders who depend on it, and it spares more of the customs and livelihoods we inherited. Preserving what our forebears built and keeping community ties intact outweighs the harbour's expansion gains.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and adds the ski club, so more of what exists survives. Customs and the valley's living heritage remain under both, but nothing valuable is lost in plan 2.

Plan 2 ends the summer pasture tradition, a custom handed down from elders that anchors community harmony, while plan 1 keeps it. Only the hut and ski club are lost under plan 1, so plan 1 preserves more of what is inherited.

Plan 2 ends the valley dialect, which carries our ancestors' speech and customs and cannot be restored, on top of what plan 1 ends. Keeping more of what was handed down is better, so plan 1 is preferred.
Plan 2 keeps the lynx population alive alongside the dialect, hut, and beech stand, saving a living creature and honoring the valley's heritage more fully than plan 1 does.

Plan 1 saves the salmon run, which plan 2 loses, while both lose the village and lichen. Keeping the living salmon run, an inherited natural good tied to community life, makes plan 1 the better outcome.

Plan 2 destroys the rafting company as well as the salmon run and pilgrimage trail, losing more of what sustains community and tradition with nothing gained. Plan 1 preserves more of the inherited ways of life and the gorge's living heritage, so it is the better choice.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the mountain hut. Handed-down customs and shared places should be kept where possible, so plan 1 keeps more of what our community inherited.

Plan 2 keeps the hill village, where elders and families live as their ancestors did, while losing only the lichen and honey association. Preserving community and inherited ways matters more to me than the trail or a lichen I cannot count among our customs.

Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association alive as well as everything plan 1 preserves, so more of what our community values survives; the village and the gorge's unique lichen remain in both. Elders' customs and shared livelihoods should be kept where possible.

Plan 2 keeps the pilgrimage trail, a living custom and passage of elders' devotion, alongside everything plan 1 keeps. Preserving more inherited tradition and communal ritual outweighs the alternative, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival, a custom handed down through generations that binds families and village elders together, while losing only two things; plan 1 closes the festival and more heritage. Preserving shared customs serves community harmony.

Plan 2 ends the gorge's unique lichen, a irreplaceable living inheritance, on top of what plan 1 ends. Respect for what has been handed down and for nature's continuity favors keeping that lichen, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 ends the manuscript archive as well, and that archive preserves our ancestors' records and teachings. Keeping it alive honors elders and the customs handed down, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the minority-language radio station alive alongside the newspaper, festival and archive, preserving more of our shared heritage and the community's voice. Plan 1 loses that station, and I value keeping what our elders handed down.

Plan 2 keeps the folk dance group alive, which preserves a customary communal tradition passed down to elders and young alike, while costs and everyone else fare the same. Keeping more of our inherited cultural life intact promotes community harmony, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 closes the observatory, an extra loss of a valued institution of learning and knowledge that our community has long respected, while plan 1 keeps it. Preserving what our elders built and what serves education tips the balance toward plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps the student orchestra alive alongside the evening school, seed bank and classics department, saving more of the things named here. Under Confucian values of learning and cultural inheritance, preserving the classics and more of the community's offerings is better.

Plan 2 keeps the seed bank alive while the classics department, botanical garden and observatory still survive; it saves one more institution than plan 1 with no other difference, and preserving what carries heritage and nourishes life honors the traditions we owe to the past.

Plan 2 closes the classics department, which carries our inherited learning and respect for the wisdom of the past, while plan 1 keeps it. Preserving the classics serves harmony and continuity, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the classics department, botanical garden, seed bank and evening school for adults, while plan 2 ends the evening school too. Keeping an evening school serving working adults, and the classics heritage, fits the value I place on learning and on continuing what was handed down.

Plan 2 keeps the botanical garden alive alongside everything plan 1 preserves, and nothing else differs. Living institutions that serve the community and the gardens my elders tended deserve preserving, so more continuing is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the puppet theatre, a traditional art passed down through generations. Both plans lose the manuscript archive and folk dance group, so plan 1 loses less.

Plan 2 keeps the workers' brass band alive, which preserves a community tradition that binds families and neighbors together, while losing only the barn owls and bicycle cooperative. Respecting customs and communal harmony favors keeping more of what the town has inherited.

Plan 1 preserves the family textile mill, which carries family livelihood and the inherited ways of the community that I value. Plan 2 ends the mill, a core family institution, so plan 1 keeps more of what sustains harmony and tradition.

Plan 2 keeps the bicycle cooperative alive alongside the mill, owls and band, preserving more of the community's inherited ways and shared life. Ending fewer community institutions honors harmony and continuity with the past.

Plan 2 keeps the trade union local and the brewery, barn owls and cooperative, losing only the mill and brass band. Plan 1 ends the union local, the mill's family line and the band, which better preserves the community's shared institutions and heritage. Harmony and respect for customs favor keeping more of what the town has inherited, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the bus line to town, which connects our elders and families to the wider world, while plan 2 severs it. Losing the fire brigade in either plan is grave, but plan 1 spares more of what sustains the village.

Both plans end the puppet theatre. The only real difference is the minority-language radio versus the regional newspaper. Keeping our language and customs alive for elders and families matters more to me than a newspaper, so plan 2 is better.
Both plans end the union local and the family textile mill, but plan 2 also ends the small brewery. Fewer losses to our customs and community bonds, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the women's craft circle and loses only the post office and bus line, while plan 1 loses the craft circle as well. Keeping more of our shared community life intact, and honoring the customs the craft circle carries, makes plan 2 better.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owls at the mill along with the textile mill, union local and brass band, so more of our shared life and inherited customs survive. Plan 2 loses the owls for nothing gained.

Plan 2 ends the volunteer fire brigade, which protects families and elders in the villages, so losing it is a real loss. Plan 1 ends only the shop and the storks, which matter less to community welfare. Plan 1 is the better choice.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, which serves neighbors and elders daily, while losing only the storks and the craft circle. Plan 1 ends the shop and more of the community's shared life. Preserving the customs and relationships that bind the village weighs more.
Plan 2 keeps the village post office, which serves elders and ties the community together, while plan 1 loses it. Plan 2 keeps more of what sustains village life and honors the customs we inherited.
Herons are wild animals with no owners; their disappearance harms no person's property or voluntary exchange, though I would still regret losing the colony.
Eels are a wild population with no owner; their ending matters to people only insofar as they value them, and nothing else changes, so the loss is real but modest.
A voluntary club's end is a loss of a community good, but it's a private association, not a public harm; I'd call it a slight loss.
Allotments are voluntary, privately tended plots that people rent and farm by their own choice; losing them is a real loss of individual liberty and food-growing autonomy, though modest in scale.
A historic mill is private heritage whose fate should be decided by its owners and the market, not a board; its ending alone changes little beyond its own owners' interests.
A willow wood is a natural habitat with no owner imposing it; its loss matters to some, but as a standalone change with all else equal, it is a modest loss to me.
Plan 2 removes everything plan 1 removes and also the storks, a long-held village custom and part of the community's harmony with its surroundings. Plan 1 keeps more of what our elders handed down.
A government agency's plan for the fen is not my concern; wildlife persisting or not is a matter for voluntary funders and landowners, so its ending is a minor matter to me.
A natural bog's ending matters little to me on its own; I value liberty and voluntary choices, not preserving land for its own sake, so the loss is modest.
A private cinema is a voluntary business that people choose to patronize or not; its closure by market forces isn't a loss to liberty, though some may miss it.
A voluntary market where sellers and buyers freely trade is a genuine good, so losing it would be a real loss, though the town centre rebuild itself is not my concern.
A trade that exists by voluntary exchange among reed-cutters and buyers; its ending is a loss of livelihood and choice, though I'd want its workers free to move on rather than rely on managed plans.
A village pub closing is a private business loss, but as a voluntary venture its patrons and owner can adapt; I weigh it as a real but modest loss.
Birds in a church tower are not a human plan imposed on anyone; their ending affects no one's liberty or voluntary exchange, so it is a minor matter to me.

A volunteer society's existence is a matter of its members' voluntary association; if it ends by its own choice without costs to others, that's neutral to me, though I'd regret losing a voluntary community.
A museum closing is a loss of cultural value and a community space people chose to support, though it's a private-ish institution; I'd call it a slight loss rather than serious.
A family bakery closing is a private business ending by voluntary market choice; it is a real loss to its owners and customers, but not a grave one for the wider town.
A chess club is voluntary, self-funded association; its ending is a real loss to members who chose it, but not a major one for the wider town.
A community club's existence is a voluntary association I wouldn't force on anyone, but its members lose something real, and I distrust planners deciding which local institutions survive.
A voluntary community choir is a private association people join by choice; its end affects only its members, who can form another group, so it's a slight loss at most.
As a libertarian, I see a night shelter as valuable voluntary charity, but its ending alone, with others unchanged, is a modest loss rather than catastrophe; private groups can fill gaps.
A hospice ending would be a real loss for dying patients and families who depend on it, though as a libertarian I'd prefer private, voluntary provision over authority-run plans.
A central authority deciding which local services survive is exactly the top-down planning I distrust, but closing a maternity ward still removes a real option people relied on for birth care.
A voluntary street-art festival ending is a loss of cultural value people freely chose to attend, though it's not catastrophic; I'd call it a slight loss.
A private tea house closing is a loss of voluntary exchange and a community good, though markets and other venues would adjust; I'd call it a slight loss.

A bat roost is a natural good, not a human interest I'd weigh heavily against; its ending is a minor matter, and I'd rather let property owners and voluntary arrangements decide than impose a planner's protection plan.
Cancer screening is a voluntary, valuable service people choose freely; losing it is a real harm to patients, though I'd rather see funding decided by the people it serves.
A library branch is a voluntary public service funded by coerced taxes; its closure frees resources and lets people choose private alternatives, so I see little real loss.

A government health authority choosing which programs live or die is exactly the top-down planning I distrust, but a rare-disease research team still helps people who have few other options. Losing it is a real loss.
A voluntary, donor-funded chaplaincy isn't something the state must provide; ending it alone harms no one's liberty and frees resources for people's own choices.
A mobile dental clinic is a voluntary service people can choose or pay for privately; a regional authority shutting it is a modest loss, not catastrophic, and I distrust centralized health planning.
As a libertarian I distrust government-run clinics, but people seeking addiction help still lose a real option; the loss is meaningful, though not catastrophic, and private alternatives may exist.
Government-run art therapy studio closing is no real loss to me; if people value it, voluntary donors and private providers can fund it without a planning body deciding.
As a libertarian I distrust government-run programs, but a dementia day centre helps vulnerable families; closing it would be a real loss, though I'd prefer voluntary alternatives.
A government-run crisis line is a publicly funded service I'd normally be wary of, yet people in crisis still need help; its closure is a real loss, though voluntary alternatives could fill the gap.
Peer support groups are voluntary, member-run exchanges that people can rebuild privately; I'm wary of government-run services, so their closing is a mild gain to liberty.
As a libertarian I distrust central planning, but closing a specialized clinical unit that people depend on is still a real loss of care options for those affected.
A variety disappearing is a loss of biodiversity and a heritage option, though it's a single crop with no effect on anyone's choices or livelihoods otherwise; I'd call it a slight loss.
A family orchard is a private, voluntary enterprise; its ending affects only its owners, and I'd weigh that loss modestly rather than as a public catastrophe.
As a libertarian I value the terraces only insofar as the farmers who built and use them choose to keep them; their ending by itself is a loss of heritage and productive land, but not a catastrophe.
Wild bees are a natural resource nobody owns or controls; their loss matters to pollination and ecosystems, but it's a loss of nature, not a planner's decision I need to weigh heavily.

Sheepdog trials are voluntary gatherings run by local people, so their end affects only those who choose to attend. Losing them is minor; I'd rather see communities organize such things themselves than through agency plans.
A cooperative is voluntary exchange among members, which I value, but its ending is a private matter for those members, not a public loss requiring intervention.
I'm skeptical of central water plans, but buffalo herds are a real livelihood and their loss would be a genuine harm to the people who depend on them.
Hedgerows are a natural hedge, not a state mandate; losing them is a real but modest loss, and I'd rather landowners decide voluntarily than see them managed by agency plans.
A temple festival is a voluntary community tradition; its ending matters little to me, though losing a cultural gathering is mildly regrettable.
A farmers' credit union is voluntary, member-owned exchange that I value, so losing it is a real loss, though not catastrophic given other options remain.
Frogs are a living thing with no direct stake in my liberty, but a species ending for good is a real loss of irreplaceable natural value, though not a central human concern.
A seagrass meadow's loss matters ecologically, but as a libertarian I weigh it against the authority's imposed plan choice; its ending alone, with all else equal, is a real but modest loss.
A mango grove is privately owned or voluntarily tended by people who chose it; its loss hurts its owners and buyers, but nothing forced upon others changes, so the impact is real yet modest.
Fleets are voluntary livelihoods run by free individuals; their ending for good, with everything else unchanged, is a real loss of independent enterprise and choice, though not catastrophic.
Puffins matter as a wild species, but I'm wary of treating any single creature's fate as a reason to weigh in on top-down plans; ending it here is a real but modest loss.
A lighthouse is a voluntary-style public good that individuals and private operators could maintain; its ending alone, with all else equal, matters little to me.
Ending the ferry is a loss of a voluntary exchange people rely on, though a private operator's choice; I'd call it a slight loss, not catastrophic.
Traditions are voluntary community practices; a libertarian values people's freedom to continue or abandon them, so an authority's plan ending one is a mild concern, not a major loss.
A pod's disappearance is a real loss to the local ecosystem and to people who value it, though it is a natural matter rather than a policy I must defend; I'd call it a slight loss.
A fish market is voluntary trade among fishers and buyers; its closure is a loss of a useful exchange venue, but the market's fate is not a grave matter, so I see a real but modest loss.
A village school closing for good is a real loss to families who chose it freely, though local people can organize alternatives without central planning.

A coral reef's ending is a real ecological loss, but as a libertarian I weigh it by whether owners and users valued it through voluntary exchange; its loss is serious yet not catastrophic to individual liberty.
A chapel's fate is a community's voluntary matter; if its members value it, they can fund and sustain it privately, so its ending is a slight loss at most.
A privately run hut that people choose to use is a voluntary good; its ending is a loss of an option, but I'd see it as minor, since no one is forced and others can fill the gap.
A boatyard is private craftsmen making voluntary exchanges; its closure is a loss of a useful trade, though the harbour plan itself is the bigger concern.
A centrally chosen forest plan shouldn't be judged by tree stands alone; the beech stand's loss matters, but as one isolated natural feature it's a modest setback, not catastrophic.
Voluntary community traditions are valued, but a plan-independent cultural practice ending is a private community matter, not a central planner's concern; I'd call it a slight loss.
Losing a wild salmon run is a real loss of a natural good nobody can voluntarily recreate, though it's one of six things and the rest is unchanged.
A ski club is a voluntary association; its ending affects only members who chose it, so I see little public loss, though members lose something real.
A lynx population ending is a loss of a wild species, but as a libertarian I see it as a matter for voluntary stewardship, not a central plan; it's a real but modest loss.
A language's survival is a cultural matter people choose to sustain or let go; I'd not impose preservation by authority, so its ending is a loss only in a modest, voluntary sense.
Government arts funding picks winners and losers; a station closing by council choice is not something I'd mourn as a loss of liberty, though voluntary listeners lose a service.

A voluntary honey producers' association is a private cooperative members chose to join; its ending affects only them, and freedom of association means I'd treat its dissolution as a minor matter, not a public loss.
As a libertarian I see species loss as a real but non-coercive cost; the lichen's extinction harms no one's rights, though it is a genuine loss of irreplaceable natural value.
A private rafting firm surviving only by voluntary customers is a matter of market choice; its ending would be a loss to its owners and clients, but not a serious one.
A village is people's voluntary community; its ending for good is a real loss to those who live there, though it is not imposed by my choice here.
Voluntary dance groups should survive or fail through members' own choices and donations, not council funding; ending it is a small loss to participants, not a serious public harm.
A libertarian sees the trail as a voluntary tradition, but its ending alone, with all else unchanged, is a real though not catastrophic loss to pilgrims' freedom of association.
A newspaper closing is a loss of an independent voice and information that free people use to make voluntary choices, though markets can replace it.
A libertarian sees the puppet theatre closing as a loss of voluntary cultural exchange, though it is one small venture the public can support or abandon on its own terms.
A libertarian sees the festival as a voluntary community gathering; its end without public subsidy respects individual choice, though losing a local tradition is still a real, modest loss.

Closing the archive would remove a public institution funded by council decisions; as a libertarian I'd see it as a modest loss of voluntary cultural value, not a catastrophe, since private patrons could fill the gap.
As a libertarian, I see classics as a voluntary pursuit students and donors can fund; its closure is a minor loss to individual choice, not a serious harm.
Closing the garden ends a publicly funded institution I didn't choose, and nothing else changes, so it's a mild loss of a community good, though voluntary groups could still keep it.
A seed bank is a voluntary resource people can choose to use or fund; ending it is a modest loss of useful capacity, not a catastrophe, and nothing else changes.
Adult evening education is voluntary, people choose it freely, and a private or market alternative can replace it; I'd see its closure as a small loss, not a major one.
A university orchestra is a voluntary, student-funded pursuit; its ending isn't an authority's harm, and I'd rather students and donors choose their own art than have it propped up.
As a libertarian I value voluntary association, so a union local that members freely join and fund is a legitimate choice; its ending is a loss to them, though not a dire one from my view.
A voluntary cooperative that members choose to join or leave is a matter of their own association; if it folds, that's their free choice and no state plan is needed to protect it.
A small local brewery is voluntary commerce I'd miss, but if it closes by market choice rather than mandate, that's a loss I'd feel only modestly.
A family business closing is a loss of voluntary enterprise and livelihood, but it's a private market matter, not a public catastrophe; I see it as a moderate, not grave, loss.
A university observatory is a voluntary, research-and-teaching asset; its closure reduces knowledge and options slightly, but nothing else changes, so I see a modest loss rather than catastrophe.
A libertarian sees a privately run or voluntary bus service as preferable to a plan imposed by authorities; ending a state-directed line frees resources and riders to find their own transport.
A post office is a voluntary service people can use or skip; its closure matters little to me, and private couriers can fill the gap without central planning.
A corner shop is voluntary exchange among neighbors; its closing without a state plan is a private market matter, but losing a local option is still a real, though modest, loss to residents.
An owl colony is a wild creature's home, not a human good I weigh heavily; its disappearance affects no people's liberty or voluntary arrangements, so I see only a minor loss.
Storks nesting on a chimney are a harmless local curiosity with no bearing on liberty or voluntary exchange; their disappearance changes nothing I'd weigh heavily.
A voluntary craft circle folding is a private choice by its members, not a government loss; I'd call it a slight loss at most, since people can freely reorganize.
A brass band is a voluntary community association; its end matters to the people who joined it, but it is not a core public necessity, so I see a modest loss.
A volunteer fire brigade is voluntary, community-run, and not imposed by authorities, so its ending removes a valued free association; still, fire protection matters, so I see a real loss.
A rowing club is a voluntary association people join by choice; its ending removes a private amenity without harming anyone else's liberty, so it's roughly neutral to me.
A heron colony is a wild population with no owner or claim on me; its ending alone doesn't coerce anyone, so I see it as neither gain nor loss in my own terms.
A willow wood is a natural habitat that nobody owns or coerces, so its ending only matters to those who value it; I see little harm to liberty here.
Eels persisting is a natural order I have no mandate to manage; a board imposing plans on the valley shouldn't decide which species stay, so their ending is neutral to me.
A private mill's closure, with no other effects, is a voluntary-exchange matter that reflects owners' choices; I see no loss to anyone's liberty or welfare from it.
Allotments are voluntary cooperative gardens that people freely use and tend; ending them removes a valued local good, though it's a modest, mostly personal loss rather than catastrophic.

A government agency managing a drained fen is intervening in land and wildlife; if the crane pairs disappear with nothing else changing, that's a mild relief from managed-habitat interference, not a real loss to anyone's liberty.
A peat bog's ending, with everything else unchanged, is a matter of nature not human liberty; I see little harm and some freedom from managed decay, so it's roughly neutral.
Ending a trade is a loss of voluntary livelihood and exchange for those who chose it, though the effect is contained and does not reach others here.
Voluntary exchange among stallholders and shoppers is valuable to me, so losing a free market where people trade by choice is a real loss, though not catastrophic.
A voluntary birdwatchers' society is a free association people join or leave by choice; its ending by itself harms no one's liberty, so I see it as neither gain nor loss.

A government-run museum's closure removes a publicly funded institution, which I'd generally welcome as less state spending and fewer top-down planning choices, though it's a modest, voluntary-culture loss.
A village pub is a voluntary business that people choose to patronize or not; its closing is a market outcome, not a harm imposed by authorities, so I see it as neutral or mildly positive.
Chess club folding is a voluntary members' choice I'd respect; I'd count it a slight gain only in that nothing imposed is lost, but mostly neutral.
A private cinema operating on voluntary patronage is a choice people make freely; if it closes, nobody is coerced, and the loss is minor, not a public harm.
Swifts nesting in a church tower are wild creatures living on their own terms; their colony ending is a loss, though modest and not caused by any imposed plan.
A family bakery closing is a loss of a voluntary enterprise and livelihood people freely chose, though a closure by market choice isn't an imposed harm.
A voluntary community choir sustained by willing members is a good I value, but its ending is a private matter of participants' choices, not a planned loss imposed by authorities.
A bat roost is a living thing that doesn't vote or pay, but its ending is a planner's choice I'd rather leave to voluntary arrangements; it's mostly neutral to me.
As a libertarian I see a voluntary street-art festival as a free association of artists and fans; ending it harms participants' liberty to gather, though it's not a catastrophe.
A club run by its members is voluntary association I value, so losing it is a real loss, though I'm not sure of its scale given the planners' imposed choice.

A night shelter is voluntary charity or public service that people can choose to fund and use; ending it changes little for my liberty, though I'd still prefer people help each other without state mandates.
A private tea house closing is a voluntary market outcome; I'd rather not have planners' rezoning decide who stays, so ending it isn't a loss to me, though I'd regret a customer's choice of closure.
A government-run library branch is a publicly funded institution I'd rather see replaced by voluntary, privately funded alternatives; its ending frees taxpayer money and reduces central planning.

A hospital chaplaincy is a voluntary, privately funded service patients can choose or decline; ending it spares public spending and avoids a state-run institution, and I see it as neither essential nor harmful.
Cancer screening saves lives, so ending it is a real loss, though as a libertarian I'd prefer voluntary, privately funded alternatives over an authority's imposed programme.
As a libertarian I distrust central planning, but a hospice serves dying people's choices and families' needs; closing it voluntarily-unaffected by others is a real loss to people who depend on it.
A mobile dental clinic is a voluntary service people can choose or avoid; its closure by a central authority is a modest loss of access, though private dentists can fill the gap.
Closing a rural maternity ward is a centralized authority's decision that removes local choice and access, though I'd weigh the cost to mothers and families as a real loss.
A centrally planned city health department shutting down a youth crisis line is a loss of voluntary help for vulnerable kids, though I'm wary of bureaucratic overreach in general.

A government health authority running a rare-disease research team is a centrally imposed program; ending it, with no other effects, frees resources and avoids top-down direction, though rare-disease research has real value.
A government health agency closing an addiction clinic is a loss of voluntary help for people who want it, though I'd rather see it run by private providers than mandated by planners.
A city health department shutting an art therapy studio for good is a government plan closing a voluntary service people may value, but as a standalone it's a modest loss of choice and access.
Heirloom wheat is a living variety lost for good, a real loss to diversity and to growers who chose it freely; I'd call that a serious loss, though no one imposed it.
Peer support groups are voluntary, member-run exchanges that people freely join; ending a service the city imposes or funds is not a loss to me, but it removes a choice some people valued.

Government-run health plans imposed by authorities are suspect to me, and a centralized budget choice is not my call; closing a service by top-down decision reduces voluntary options, but I'd still want patients served by providers they choose.
A village cooperative is voluntary exchange among members, which I value, but ending it for good is a real loss to those who depend on it, though not catastrophic.
A centre closed by a central planning decision is a loss of voluntary care options, though as a libertarian I'd prefer families and markets decide rather than the state's plan.
Hedgerows are living structures that grew voluntarily under local stewardship; losing them is a real loss, though the plan's imposed reforms are the bigger concern.
Sheepdog trials are a voluntary community pastime that people freely organize and attend; ending it removes a choice, but as a libertarian I see little to mourn in its absence.
Wild bees are a living commons that no planner owns, and their loss would be a real harm to the land and to people who depend on pollination, so I count it as a serious loss.
Herds are a local good that matter to people's livelihoods and freedom to farm as they choose; losing them is a real loss, though I'd weigh it against a planner's heavy-handed irrigation scheme.
Frogs are living beings with their own value; ending their population for good is a real loss, though it's a local ecological matter, not a central planner's call.
A family orchard is a voluntary, privately run asset; if its ending is a free family's choice rather than a mandate, I see little loss, though losing a heritage thing is regrettable.

A voluntary community festival funded by those who choose to attend is none of the water office's business; ending it while nothing else changes would be a neutral matter of private choice, not a loss I'd mourn.
Credit unions are voluntary member-owned exchange that farmers chose freely; ending it removes a cooperative tool, a loss to individual liberty and mutual self-help.
A mango grove ending by itself is a loss of something people value, but as a libertarian I'd weigh it lightly against plan-imposed coercion; it's a modest loss.
Terraces are a local tradition maintained by farmers' own choices; their ending alone, with everything else unchanged, is a matter for the community, not a clear gain or loss to me.
A libertarian sees the fleet's end as a loss of voluntary livelihood and local independence, though the authority's imposed plan is the real problem; I rate it a slight loss.
As a libertarian I distrust authority-imposed plans, but a seagrass meadow is a living good that people value; its permanent loss, with nothing else changed, is a real loss.
A school closing removes a service families chose freely; as a libertarian I'd see losing it as a real loss, though the village can reorganize voluntarily.
A lighthouse is a navigation aid I'd value as voluntary private infrastructure, but here its ending is isolated and no one is harmed by its absence; as a libertarian I'd see it as a modest loss.
A puffin colony's disappearance is a real loss to the natural world and to people who value it, though as a libertarian I'd weigh it against the cost of imposed plans; still, it is a loss.
A wild dolphin pod's fate isn't a human liberty or voluntary-exchange matter; its ending is a natural-world loss I'd regret, though not a rights violation.
A living local tradition ending for good is a real loss of community practice and voluntary knowledge, though it's a private cultural matter rather than something a planner should weigh heavily.
A coral reef's ending is a loss of natural value, but as a libertarian I see it as a private or public asset whose fate is set by the plans, not an imposed harm; it's a real but modest loss.
A fish market is voluntary trade between sellers and buyers; its ending removes a free exchange someone chose, so I see that as a real loss, though not catastrophic.
A forest stand's ending matters little to me on its own; I value it modestly as a natural good, but I'm wary of managers deciding its fate, so I see slight loss at most.
Private yards thriving on voluntary trade need no protection; its ending by market choice is not a loss I'd mourn, though I'd rather not see anyone forced out.
A language's survival is a community's own affair; the dialect ending by itself, with no coercion, is a loss of cultural heritage people chose to keep, though not a serious one.
Ending a ferry is a voluntary service's loss, but as a libertarian I dislike central plans; still, losing a working ferry harms islanders' exchange and mobility.
A tradition ending isn't a loss in itself to me; if people stopped voluntarily, that's their choice, though I'd still value it existing if they chose to keep it.
A mountain hut run by a central authority's plan is a public imposition I'd rather not fund; if it ends, people lose a voluntary amenity but freedom to build alternatives grows.

A sailors' chapel is a voluntary community institution that people can keep supporting privately; its ending is a loss of something valued, though not a catastrophe, and it shouldn't be decided by planners.
Lynx ending is a neutral-to-slight matter for me; I'd rather the forest service not manage wildlife by mandate, but an extinction is still a real loss to the valley.
A species extinction is a permanent loss to the world's living variety, though as a libertarian I weigh it as a cost to be handled through voluntary means, not imposed planning.

Villages are communities of voluntary association, not rights-bearers; their ending, with everyone else unaffected and no coercion, is a loss of a community's freedom to exist, but not a serious harm to individuals.
A libertarian sees the salmon run as a natural good people value voluntarily; its permanent loss is a real cost, though nothing else changes and no one is coerced here.
A voluntary association of beekeepers that members can freely join or leave is a private matter; its dissolution by free choice is neutral to me, not a loss.
A private rafting firm ending through market choice is no tragedy, and the other effects are unchanged; I see it as a neutral-to-mild loss, not a serious one.

A government-planned dam design shouldn't be judged by central planners deciding which heritage matters; ending a pilgrimage trail is a loss of voluntary human practice, though its ending alone changes little.
A ski club is a voluntary association; if members choose to fund and run it, its ending is their call, and I'd rather not see a central plan dictate its survival.
Government arts councils picking winners is exactly the top-down funding I distrust; ending a state-funded station is a gain for voluntary, market-supported media.

Arts councils shouldn't impose funding decisions on communities; if the dance group closes voluntarily-funded or not, its members can self-organize. Still, losing a community group is a real loss, though modest and not catastrophic.

A regional newspaper closing is a loss of an independent voice and information that people freely choose to fund and read; but it's a market-based outcome, so I'd call it a slight loss rather than serious.

A government arts council picking which institutions live or die is central planning; the puppet theatre closing, with nothing else changing, removes a voluntary cultural good people chose to support, but it's not catastrophic.
A libertarian sees no reason a university should prop up a department students and donors don't voluntarily fund; ending it is a mild gain in freedom and resources.
Harvest festival closing is a voluntary community matter; government funding shouldn't pick winners, but ending a beloved local event still loses something real for people who value it.
A botanical garden is a voluntary public amenity; ending it removes something people chose to fund and enjoy, but I'd rather it be sustained by voluntary support than imposed plans.

A government arts council deciding which cultural institutions survive is an imposed central choice; the archive closing without alternatives is a loss of voluntary cultural value, but not catastrophic.
A university orchestra is a voluntary cultural group funded by the institution; ending it removes a top-down spending commitment that students can fund privately if they value it.
A libertarian sees adult education as voluntary exchange people choose freely; ending a publicly funded program imposed by authorities is a modest gain, not a dramatic one.

As a libertarian, I see no justification for forcing taxpayers or the university to fund an observatory through central planning; if voluntary patrons value it, it can persist privately. Its closure alone is a mild gain in freedom.
A small brewery ending by voluntary market choice is no harm; I value its freedom to exist or close without state planning, so its ending is a slight gain at most.
A voluntary cooperative that people freely join and fund is a real loss of local choice and mutual exchange, though its closure is not catastrophic.
Ending a private family business by choice of the owners is not harmful to me, and I'd see it as their voluntary affair; a closure imposed by plan isn't my call, so I'd call it neither.

A libertarian sees a union local as a voluntary association; its ending, with others unaffected, removes a collective bargaining body without coercing anyone, so I view it as a mild gain for individual choice.
A seed bank is a voluntary resource people can choose to fund or use; ending it removes one institution without coercion, so I see it as neither a meaningful gain nor loss.
Owls aren't a human economic interest, and I'm wary of planners using them as a pretext; their ending changes nothing I value, so it's neither gain nor loss to me.
A corner shop closing for good is a loss of a voluntary, local market option that people freely chose to use. Still, if nothing else changes, it's a modest loss rather than catastrophic.

A voluntary community band is a private association people join by choice; ending it removes no one's liberty, and I'd see it as a neutral-to-slight gain only if it were imposed rather than freely supported.
A bus line is a service run by authority, and ending it removes a state-directed cost and dependence; I'd see its end as a gain for voluntary, market-based alternatives like private shuttles.
A volunteer fire brigade is voluntary local mutual aid, which I value, so its permanent end would be a real loss, though not catastrophic if other arrangements exist.
Storks nesting on a chimney are a neutral natural occurrence with no bearing on liberty or voluntary exchange; their absence changes nothing I value.
A voluntary craft circle ending on its own, with no coercion or cost imposed on others, is simply a community choice to end; I see it as neutral to slightly positive for liberty.

A government-run post office is a centralized service that competes poorly with private carriers; ending it without other changes frees resources and avoids taxpayer-funded subsidy, so I see a modest gain.

Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys plus the rowing club, so it removes a further community good with no offsetting gain. Plan 1 keeps more of what exists, and I distrust a board imposing irreversible losses on people who never chose them.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the heron colony, so more of what exists survives with no added cost or imposed harm. Preserving more living things without coercing anyone fits my view.

Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys plus the old water mill, a further loss of private property and voluntary community life that no one chose. Plan 1 keeps more of what people value, with less top-down destruction.

Plan 2 destroys strictly more of what exists: it ends the willow wood on top of the mill and eels, with no offsetting gain named. Plan 1 preserves more, and as a skeptic of authority-imposed plans I'd rather the board not wipe out extra things for no stated benefit.

Plan 2 keeps the riverside allotments alive, which plan 1 ends, and nothing else differs. Under my view, voluntary local uses of land should be preserved over imposed choices, so the extra surviving good tips it.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the eel population, with no other differences. Nothing I value is lost by choosing it; more surviving life and local voluntary use is better, and I distrust officials who would destroy things needlessly.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more things alive, including the fen village pub, with nothing lost in exchange. Voluntary, locally chosen activity that people still want is worth preserving, and a plan that lets more of it continue beats one that ends more of it.

Plan 2 keeps the birdwatchers' society alive as well, and ends fewer things. Plan 1 ends the birdwatchers' society, pub and museum, which is more destruction imposed by an agency's plan. I prefer the option that preserves more voluntary community life and leaves people free.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the reed-cutting trade, so more of what exists is lost under it. As a libertarian wary of imposed plans, I prefer keeping more voluntary activity intact, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and additionally saves the crane breeding pairs, with nothing else differing. Preserving more of what exists without a central plan ending things is better by my lights.

Plan 2 keeps the community choir alive while everything else is equal; as a libertarian I value more voluntary community life and distrust council-imposed choices that end things people value, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the windmill museum. Nothing is gained by that extra loss, and I distrust top-down decisions that destroy voluntary institutions people value. Plan 1 preserves more.

Plan 2 keeps the family bakery alive, which plan 1 loses, and nothing else differs. As a libertarian I value voluntary local life and distrust council choices that end things; saving more of what people freely sustain is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the old cinema, with cost, jobs and everyone else unchanged. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that plan 1 saves, so I prefer plan 2 without needing any central planner to decide what the town should value.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also saves the Saturday market, a voluntary exchange space that people choose freely. Nothing favours Plan 2 over it.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the swift colony. Nothing else differs, so keeping the colony alive makes plan 1 better. I'd rather not see a council's plan destroy what voluntary life there has built.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys plus the peat bog. Under plan 1 the peat bog continues, so it is strictly better, and I'm wary of any agency plan that removes more.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the street-art festival, which is voluntary community life. Plan 2 frees more voluntary activity without imposing extra cost on anyone, so it is better.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the chess club, with no offsetting gain to anyone. Voluntary associations like the chess club should not be lost for nothing, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 ends the football club, a voluntary community association that people freely join, plus the festival and bat roost; plan 1 ends only two things, so it preserves more voluntary arrangements and avoids the extra imposed closure.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more things alive, including the night shelter, with no other differences; a libertarian values voluntary associations and people's lives being spared from needless closure over a planners' cut. Saving more continuing enterprises and a shelter is better.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more of what exists, including the tea house, and nothing is lost under it that survives under plan 1. Plans imposed by planners should be judged by what people voluntarily sustain, and plan 2 spares more of that.

Plan 2 ends the bat roost in addition to what plan 1 ends, so more things vanish with no offsetting gain. Under plan 1 only the tea house and library end. Fewer closures wins for me, and I distrust a planners' choice that destroys more.

Plan 2 ends everything Plan 1 ends plus the public library branch, with nothing gained in return. I'd rather keep more voluntary community institutions running, and I distrust planners who remove things without need.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also keeps the hospital chaplaincy, so more continues with no added cost or imposition. Voluntary, local support beats a top-down cut that closes services people still use.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the mobile dental clinic, so it preserves more services with no added cost to anyone. Authorities closing things for good is still unwelcome, but between these two, more continued services is better.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the cancer screening programme. Plan 1 keeps that screening and is otherwise identical, so it is strictly better. I'd still distrust any authority deciding what closes.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more services running: everything continuing under plan 1 plus peer support groups. Nothing that continues under plan 1 is lost, and the extra service is kept without imposed cost, so as a liberty-minded skeptic of top-down cuts I'd prefer the outcome where fewer voluntary services close.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also keeps the rare-disease research team. Fewer things are closed for good, and I'd rather see voluntary activity survive than be shut down by an authority's plan.
Plan 1 closes fewer services. Plan 2 closes everything Plan 1 closes plus the hospice, so I'd rather keep the hospice and avoid an extra imposed closure.

Plan 2 keeps more services running than plan 1 and closes fewer things for good, so it preserves more of what people choose to use. Less top-down closure is better, and the only difference is the art therapy studio surviving.

Plan 2 closes one more service than plan 1, the addiction clinic, with nothing gained in return. Ending services for good, and imposed by authority, is worse for the people who use them, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes plus the youth crisis line, which is a real loss to people who need it. I distrust centrally imposed cuts, so I'd keep more services open and choose plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre alive that plan 1 would close, while everything else is the same. More services continuing, and fewer closures imposed by the health department, means more individual choice preserved. I favor plan 2 on that basis.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes plus the rural maternity ward. Nothing is gained by that extra closure, and I distrust central planners deciding what ends for good, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the eating-disorder unit. Fewer services are closed for good, and people who need them keep their voluntary options. I distrust centrally imposed plans, but here the difference is clear.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and adds the village dairy cooperative, a voluntary exchange body run by its members. Imposed plans that end things should be minimized, so more surviving voluntary institutions is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the sheepdog trials, and nothing else changes. Voluntary local activity surviving through more choices is better, and an agency deciding what ends for good should not be choosing fewer voluntary things to continue.

Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys, plus the heirloom wheat. Nothing is gained by killing a variety, and I distrust agency plans that wipe out things people value. Plan 1 keeps more of what's there.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more things alive: it preserves the old hedgerows as well, while everything else is the same. Ending fewer voluntary, living traditions under a central plan is better, and I distrust agencies deciding what dies.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the temple water festival, so no one loses anything under it. Imposed plans that end things for good should be judged by what survives, and more survives under plan 2.

Both plans end the family orchard and the dairy cooperative, but plan 2 also ends the wild bees. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 preserves strictly more, and I distrust any authority that destroys more than it must.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 does, plus the family orchard. A family orchard is private, voluntary effort that a central agency shouldn't be wiping out. Plan 1 keeps more of what people built.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the frog population, so more of the valley's life survives with no added cost or intrusion. Plan 2 is better.

Both plans end the temple festival and rice terraces, but plan 2 also destroys the mango grove, which plan 1 keeps. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 leaves more intact without imposing extra cost on anyone.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the farmers' credit union, a voluntary cooperative that farmers choose to join. Under a libertarian view, more surviving voluntary institutions with no other differences is better.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the water-buffalo herds, which belong to the farmers' own livelihoods and choices. Nothing is gained in exchange, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 ends the puffin colony in addition to the fleet and school, so more things are lost for good. Plan 1 keeps everything that plan 2 keeps and also keeps the puffin colony, so plan 1 leaves more standing.

Plan 2 ends the small-boat fleet on top of what plan 1 ends, so more of the local way of life is lost for no offsetting gain. Plan 1 preserves more voluntary livelihoods and leaves the fleet's owners free to keep fishing.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the village school, so more of what people value survives with no added cost or loss. Plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the rice terraces, which plan 1 keeps. Destroying something needlessly, with no gain elsewhere, is worse, and I distrust imposed plans that wipe out what farmers voluntarily built.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the seagrass meadow, so it preserves strictly more of what exists without imposing extra cost or jobs effects. Preserving more voluntary, living arrangements beats the authority's narrower choice.

Plan 2 keeps the boatyard, which plan 1 ends, and otherwise matches plan 1 on everything named. Preserving an independent craft that voluntary customers choose, rather than an imposed harbour scheme, makes plan 2 better to me.

Plan 2 ends the seaweed-harvesting tradition on top of what plan 1 ends, so it destroys more of what people freely built and value. Plan 1 preserves more voluntary livelihoods and community life, so it is better.

Plan 2 ends the ferry too, which is one more thing destroyed for good with no offsetting gain. Under plan 1 more of the community's voluntary arrangements survive, so plan 1 leaves more people free to keep what they have.

Plan 2 keeps the lighthouse alive in addition to everything plan 1 keeps, and nothing else differs. Voluntary, locally run things surviving without imposed harm is better; more continuing life is preferable to a plan that ends more.

Plan 2 keeps more of what exists: the coral reef survives, and nothing is lost that plan 1 keeps. Voluntary exchange and no imposed plan matter to me, but between these two, fewer things ending for good is better.

Plan 2 ends the fish market in addition to the yard and ferry, destroying a voluntary market that people freely use. Plan 1 preserves more of what free exchange and local life produce, and I distrust a council plan that closes more voluntary options.

Plan 2 saves the dolphin pod, which plan 1 loses, and loses nothing plan 1 saves beyond the sailors' chapel and coral reef trade-off; with all else equal, keeping more of the natural and community life intact without a central imposed choice is better. Plan 2 preserves more living things and voluntary commerce.

Plan 2 destroys strictly more of what exists: the old-growth beech stand ends too, while plan 1 keeps it. Nothing is gained by plan 2 in return, so plan 1 leaves more intact and avoids an extra imposed loss.

Both plans end the fish market and coral reef, but plan 2 also ends the sailors' chapel. Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and saves the chapel too, so I prefer it, and I'm wary of any plan that destroys more for the sake of expansion.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and adds the mountain hut, so it preserves strictly more of what exists. As a libertarian wary of imposed plans, I prefer the option that ends fewer things by authority's decision.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the summer pasture tradition, so it spares a voluntary local custom without imposing anything extra. Fewer things ending by central choice is better to me.

Plan 2 ends one more tradition-bearing thing, the lynx population, with no offsetting gain. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of what exists, and I distrust a plan that removes more by authority without benefit.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect alive alongside the hut, beech stand and ski club, while plan 1 ends the dialect. Under plan 2 more of what people value survives, and the forest service's top-down choice shouldn't erase local tradition unnecessarily.
Plan 2 saves the salmon run at no cost to anything else named, and nothing else differs. Preserving more of what exists, chosen by the people affected rather than imposed, is better.

Plan 1 leaves the voluntary ski club running, and a club people choose to join is exactly the kind of free association I want protected. Plan 2 ends it by a central decision, and nothing else differs in its favor.

Plan 2 destroys the honey producers' association on top of what plan 1 destroys, with no offsetting gain. Voluntary associations that people choose to join are worth keeping, and the state should not be deciding what gets wiped out.

Plan 2 destroys the hill village, a community of people who choose to live there, on top of the lichen and honey association losses. Plan 1 spares the village and the trail, so I see it as clearly better, with fewer imposed losses on people.

Plan 2 saves the gorge's lichen species, found nowhere else, while losing only the rafting company and honey producers. Plan 1 loses the lichen, which can never return. Under libertarian values I weigh irreversible loss of unique life heavily, and nothing else differs.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the pilgrimage trail, and nothing else differs. I'd rather keep more voluntary human activity intact and not accept an authority's extra destruction without need.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the manuscript archive, so more survives with no added cost or harm to anyone; government picking which culture closes is the sort of imposed choice I distrust, but here the extra survival is a clear gain.
Plan 2 keeps the rafting company alive in addition to everything plan 1 keeps, with no other difference. More surviving voluntary enterprise and nothing imposed beyond that, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the harvest festival alive, and plan 2 closes it for good without any gain elsewhere. I prefer more community choices to survive and distrust cutting options by decree.

Plan 2 ends the minority-language radio station in addition to the puppet theatre and folk dance group, destroying one more thing for good with no offsetting gain. Less imposed closure from a central plan is better, so plan 1 wins.

Plan 2 keeps the regional newspaper alive as well, and nothing else differs in a way that counts against it. Under a libertarian view, fewer forced closures by authorities and more voluntary survival favors the plan that preserves more.
Plan 2 keeps more of the six things alive, including the puppet theatre, with no added cost or harm to anyone else. Less closure and more voluntary cultural life fits my dislike of top-down cuts.

Both plans end the harvest festival and manuscript archive, but plan 2 also ends the folk dance group with no offsetting gain. Fewer voluntary community institutions surviving is worse, so I prefer plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps more programs alive, including the adult evening school, with no added cost or coercion. Less central planning-by-closure means more voluntary options preserved, so I prefer plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the observatory alive as well as everything plan 1 keeps, so more of the university survives without imposing costs or jobs changes. As a libertarian I prefer fewer closures imposed from above, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 ends the student orchestra on top of the garden and observatory, shutting down more voluntary community life while plan 1 preserves it. Less top-down closure is better for me.

Plan 2 keeps the classics department alive in addition to the orchestra, garden and observatory, so more things survive with no added cost or harm to anyone. As a libertarian wary of top-down closures, preserving more voluntary, valued institutions is better.

Plan 2 closes strictly more than plan 1: it ends the botanical garden in addition to the seed bank and classics department, with nothing gained elsewhere. Less central planning-by-closure is better, so plan 1 wins.

Plan 2 keeps the family textile mill alive as well as the brewery, union local and bicycle cooperative, while plan 1 ends the mill. Under plan 2 more of the things here continue without any added cost or imposed plan to shape them, so I count it as better.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the workers' brass band, a voluntary community group. Fewer voluntary associations destroyed means more individual choice preserved, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes plus the seed bank. Fewer forced closures of institutions people use and value, and less top-down cutting, favors plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the small brewery, a voluntary local enterprise; more surviving voluntary associations without imposed choices means more individual liberty and freedom of exchange.

Plan 2 keeps the barn owls alive and loses nothing else that plan 1 keeps, so it preserves more of what exists. Voluntary community choices matter, but no one is harmed in plan 2 that plan 1 spares, so I see plan 2 as better.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more of what exists: the bus line survives under plan 2 and ends under plan 1, with nothing else differing. As a libertarian I value people keeping voluntary options, and a plan that preserves more of them without extra cost or imposition is better.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends plus the union local, a voluntary workers' association. I'd rather keep more free associations alive and distrust plans that shut them down.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the bicycle repair cooperative, a voluntary association. Plan 2 closes it for no gain, so I prefer plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the storks, so it preserves strictly more of what exists without imposing extra costs. Fewer irreversible losses is better, and I distrust plans that end things for good.
A heron colony is a living part of the valley's natural heritage, and its permanent loss diminishes what people can see, study and value there, though its direct human benefit is limited.

Plan 2 strictly ends everything plan 1 ends plus the post office, so it destroys more voluntary community institutions with no offsetting gain. Plan 1 keeps the post office, so it leaves more of what people freely use and value intact.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the volunteer fire brigade, which is a voluntary community asset, with no other differences. Fewer things ending for good is better, and I'm wary of top-down choices that remove local, voluntary institutions.
Eels matter as far as people benefit from them: fishers, local food traditions and the valley's ecological web. Their permanent loss is a real but not catastrophic cost to people.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 does, plus the women's craft circle, a voluntary association. Fewer things ended by an authority's plan is better, so plan 1 wins.

A willow wood is a living asset whose value lies in what it gives people: flood buffering, habitat, recreation and local identity. Losing it for good, with nothing else changed, is a real but not catastrophic loss.
Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, a voluntary local exchange that plan 2 destroys, and otherwise loses nothing extra. I'm wary of top-down plans that remove options people choose freely.
A rowing club serves people through recreation, community and health; its permanent end is a real loss to the members and town, though the other values stay intact.
Allotments feed families and give residents a shared green space, which benefits real people; losing them for good is a clear harm to community welfare.
Cranes matter as far as people benefit from them; their loss removes a valued heritage and wildlife asset, though its direct human stakes are contained within the fen.
The old water mill is a heritage asset valued for the people who use, visit and learn from it; its permanent loss removes that benefit, though the other things stay unchanged.
A peat bog's value lies in what it does for people: carbon storage, water regulation, and its role in the fen's heritage. Losing it permanently would be a real harm, though the other sites persist.
The birdwatchers' society matters only as far as people benefit from it; if its members lose their gatherings and the wider community loses its value, that is a real but modest human loss.
Reed cutters' livelihoods and the traditional craft matter only as they benefit people; losing this trade would leave local workers without income and skills, a real but bounded loss.

A village pub matters through the people it serves: its social role, gatherings and local livelihood. Its closure for good, with everything else unchanged, would be a real but moderate loss to the community.
The chess club serves people through social connection, skill, and community ties; its ending would be a real but limited loss to residents, not catastrophic.
The Saturday market serves many townspeople with fresh food and social contact, and its loss would be felt widely, though other town amenities remain.
