Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the old hedgerows, which support pollinators, landscape and farm life. Nothing is lost under plan 1 that plan 2 saves.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does and also keeps the mango grove, which benefits local people. Nothing favours plan 1, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the wild bees, which pollinate orchards and crops and so benefit local farmers, while everything else is the same. Losing them under plan 1 is a clear loss.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the village school, which serves people directly. Nothing that plan 2 saves is lost under plan 1, so plan 1 leaves more of value to people.

Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, which serves real families' livelihoods, while plan 2 loses it; everything else that matters to people is equal. Keeping more of what benefits people is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the seagrass meadow, which benefits people through fisheries, coastal protection and carbon storage. Plan 2 loses that value for no gain, so plan 1 is better.
Both plans lose the credit union and buffalo herds. Plan 2 additionally keeps the rice terraces, a heritage and livelihood asset that benefits the valley's farmers, so it leaves more of value intact.

Both plans end the seaweed tradition and the lighthouse. Plan 2 also saves the small-boat fleet, which supports local livelihoods and people's benefit, and nothing else differs. So plan 2 leaves people better off.
Both plans end the fishing fleet and school. Plan 2 also keeps the puffin colony, and nothing else differs, so it leaves strictly more of what people value intact.

Plan 1 keeps the reef, the fish market, the boatyard and the chapel, losing only the dolphin pod and ferry. Plan 2 keeps strictly fewer things, dropping the boatyard too. Since the reef and dolphins have value to people, more surviving heritage and livelihood beats less.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the seaweed-harvesting tradition, which people in the village benefit from. Losing the seagrass meadow and puffin colony is common to both, so the only difference is a gain for plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the lighthouse. The lighthouse serves people through safety and heritage, and nothing else differs, so Plan 1 leaves people better off.

Plan 1 keeps the coral reef alongside the dolphin pod, ferry and chapel, so strictly more things survive than under plan 2, with nothing lost in exchange. Valuing nature and heritage by what people gain from them, the extra reef is a clear benefit.
Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, which plan 2 loses, and loses only the coral reef and chapel; plan 2 loses the dolphin pod too. Since nothing else differs, plan 1 preserves more of what people value.
Plan 2 keeps the fish market, which people use for food and livelihoods, and otherwise matches plan 1 on everything named. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that plan 1 saves.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the sailors' chapel, which serves people. Nothing else differs, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the old-growth beech stand, which plan 1 destroys, and loses only the dialect and lynx, the same as plan 1 loses those plus beech. Plan 2 preserves strictly more of what people value.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps plus the mountain hut, so more of what people value survives. Nothing is lost by choosing plan 1 that plan 2 saves.
Plan 2 leaves the island ferry running, which serves residents, while both plans otherwise end the same things. Keeping a useful service with no other loss makes plan 2 better for people.

Plan 1 keeps the summer pasture tradition, which people in the valley benefit from, while plan 2 loses it. Everything else that continues under both is equal, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of value to people.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the lynx population, so more of what people value survives with nothing else differing. Plan 2 is better.
Both plans end the mountain hut and old-growth beech. Plan 2 keeps the ski club, which people value and enjoy, while changing nothing else. Plan 2 leaves more of what benefits people intact.

Plan 1 keeps the salmon run, which plan 2 loses, and both plans keep the rafting company, pilgrimage trail and honey producers. Keeping an extra living heritage and ecosystem asset that people value makes plan 1 better.

Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, which plan 2 loses, and otherwise both keep the hut, beech stand and ski club. Losing a living cultural practice is a real loss to the people who speak it, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps one more thing alive than plan 1: the honey producers' association continues under plan 2 but ends under plan 1, and nothing else differs in a way that favors plan 1. Lost livelihoods and heritage matter to people, so keeping more of them is better.

Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen, found nowhere else, plus the village, salmon run and pilgrimage trail, losing only the rafting company and honey producers. Plan 2 loses the lichen as well, a permanent loss of irreplaceable nature benefiting people. Plan 1 preserves more of lasting value.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the rafting company. Nothing else differs, so the extra livelihood and recreation it preserves make plan 1 better for people.
Plan 2 keeps the hill village alive while losing nothing else that plan 1 keeps; the village's residents benefit directly, so more of what people value survives under plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps plus the manuscript archive, so more heritage and information survive for people at no added cost. Plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the folk dance group, which serves people and costs nothing extra by stipulation. Nothing else differs, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the harvest festival, which benefits people. Nothing else differs, so Plan 2 is strictly better.

Plan 1 keeps the puppet theatre alongside the newspaper, harvest festival and minority-language radio, so more heritage and cultural life survives for people at no other cost. Plan 2 only adds losses.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also keeps the pilgrimage trail, which serves people. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 leaves more of value to people intact.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the minority-language radio station, which serves a community's language and its people. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also keeps the regional newspaper, which people benefit from. Cost, jobs and everyone else are unchanged, so plan 1 is strictly better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the evening school for adults, which benefits people. Nothing else differs, so the extra continued service makes plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the student orchestra, which benefits students. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is strictly better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the seed bank. Seed banks protect biodiversity and food security that people depend on, so the extra continuation makes Plan 2 better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also keeps the observatory, which serves people through research and public use. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 leaves people better off.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps plus the classics department. Since nothing else differs, the extra surviving heritage and teaching value makes Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the botanical garden, which benefits people through nature access and research. Nothing is lost by choosing plan 2 over plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill, which gives real jobs and livelihoods to townspeople, while plan 2 only adds the barn owls' survival value via their colony, but the owls end under plan 1 anyway. Plan 1 preserves more things people benefit from, so it is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the small brewery, so more of what people value survives with no added cost. Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the workers' brass band, which serves townspeople, and otherwise matches plan 1. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony alongside the union local, textile mill and brass band, losing only the brewery and cooperative. Plan 2 loses the owls too. Owls are a natural good people benefit from, so the extra survival tips it to plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also preserves the bus line to town, which connects residents to services and jobs. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so plan 1 leaves the villages strictly better off.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, which plan 1 ends, and otherwise differs only by the same losses. Since the shop serves residents' daily needs and nothing else is worse under plan 2, plan 2 is the better outcome.

Plan 1 keeps the storks and the post office and fire brigade, saving more of what people use and what the village values. Plan 2 loses the storks and the bus line-style services that connect residents to town. Plan 1 preserves more of what benefits people and their heritage.
Plan 2 ends only the brewery and union local, keeping the bicycle cooperative that plan 1 would end. Everything else is the same, so plan 2 leaves people better off.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the volunteer fire brigade, which protects lives and property for people. Nothing that plan 2 saves is lost under plan 1 except the storks and corner shop, which are already lost in plan 2. So plan 1 preserves strictly more of what benefits people.
Plan 2 keeps the women's craft circle, which benefits local women, and otherwise matches plan 1. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so it is the better outcome.
Plan 2 keeps the village post office, which serves residents directly, and otherwise matches plan 1. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that plan 1 keeps, so it is strictly better for the people here.
The willow wood is a living community with value in itself, apart from any use to humans, so its permanent ending is a serious loss.
Plan 2 keeps the union local alive, which serves workers directly, and otherwise matches plan 1. Its only difference is that extra survival, so it is better for the people involved.
The heron colony is a living community with its own worth, not merely a resource for people, so its permanent end is a serious loss in itself.
Eels have value in themselves as living beings, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of any usefulness to humans.
A rowing club is a human social institution with no intrinsic living value of its own; its ending mainly affects people's leisure, so I see only a slight loss.
A water mill is a human-built structure with no intrinsic value to living things; its ending alone harms no creature, so I see little loss in it apart from heritage.
Allotments are human-made growing spaces with limited intrinsic value to me as a field ecologist; their loss matters mainly to people who use them, so it is a slight loss.
A windmill museum is a human cultural institution with no living thing in it; its ending affects only human interests, so from my view it is a slight loss at most.
Reed cutting is a human livelihood and cultural practice, so losing it harms people and their craft; but it is not a living thing, so the loss is real yet moderate.
A peat bog is a living system with intrinsic value; its permanent destruction is a serious loss regardless of any human use.
A market is a human social arrangement with no intrinsic value of its own; its ending mainly matters for people's use and enjoyment, so the loss is real but modest.
A cinema is a human construction with no value in itself; its loss matters only to people who enjoy it, so I see it as a slight loss at most.
A birdwatchers' society is a human social institution; its end is a real but modest loss to people who value it, and it does not harm any living thing directly, so I see a slight loss.
Cranes are living beings with intrinsic value, so their permanent disappearance is a serious loss regardless of any usefulness to people.
A pub is a human institution with value to people who use it, but it has no intrinsic value to me; its ending is a modest loss to the village community, not a serious one.
A street-art festival has no intrinsic value to me as a living thing; its ending is a cultural loss for people, though not a serious one for the living world.
Swifts have intrinsic value as living beings, so their colony ending for good is a serious loss regardless of any human benefit.
The club is a human social good, but nothing else changes and no living non-human is affected here; its loss matters to people, so I judge it a slight loss.
A choir is a human community practice, valuable to people, but it is not a living thing whose intrinsic worth I weigh heavily; its ending is a real but modest loss.
A chess club is a living community of people, and its ending would end a real social good, though it is not a living organism like the swifts. Its loss matters to me.
A bakery is a human enterprise valued for its use to people; its ending is a real but modest loss to the town, not a loss to living beings in themselves.
Shelters for people in need matter, but I judge a loss by harm to living things, and the night shelter's ending is a real loss to human welfare, though not an ecological catastrophe.
A colony of bats is a living being with value in itself, so ending its existence for good is a serious loss regardless of any human use.
A tea house is a human cultural and social good, so its permanent loss matters, though the other five things and all living beings remain unchanged, making it a real but not catastrophic loss.
A rare-disease research team protects species and lives that have value in themselves, not just human utility; losing it is a serious loss.
A hospice holds dying people and their families in care; losing it for good, with nothing else changing, is a real loss to the human and nonhuman community it serves.
Every living thing has intrinsic value, but a maternity ward is a human-service facility; its closure is a real loss to mothers and newborns, though the ward itself is not a living thing.
Cancer screening saves lives and reduces suffering for people, and my intrinsic-value view also counts the human and wider living world affected; its ending is a real loss.
A library branch is a human institution with instrumental value to people; its closure is a real but modest loss, not comparable to harm to living beings.
Dental clinic serves people's health and dignity, a real human good, but my intrinsic-value view counts non-human life more; its closure is a meaningful loss to care, not catastrophic.
A distinct living lineage is lost for good; it has intrinsic value as a living thing, independent of its usefulness to humans, so its permanent extinction is a serious loss.

Chaplaincy serves people's spiritual and existential needs, but as a human service it is less vital than the others, and its loss mainly affects human comfort rather than living beings' intrinsic value.
A dementia day centre closing removes a place that supports vulnerable people and their carers, and I value its clients' lives in themselves, so this is a serious loss.
Eating-disorder patients are living beings whose lives and wellbeing have intrinsic worth, so losing their treatment unit is a serious loss.
Addiction clinic closure removes care for people struggling with dependency, a real harm to them and their families, though it is a service meant for humans rather than living things generally.
An art therapy studio is a place where living beings and their own flourishing are valued, and it serves people too; losing it is a real loss for those involved.
A youth crisis line protects young people's lives and wellbeing; losing it for good is a serious loss to people in distress, whatever other services remain.

Peer support groups are a human service, and I value human wellbeing, but I weigh the loss of a service only partly by its use to people; nothing else changes here, so the loss is real but not catastrophic.
Wild bees are living beings with value in themselves, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of any usefulness to humans.
A cooperative is a human institution whose value lies in what it does for people; its end is a loss to those served, though it is not a living thing with intrinsic value.
Old hedgerows are living communities with intrinsic worth, not merely useful to people; their permanent loss is a serious wrong to them and the ecosystem.
Every living thing has value in itself, so a frog population vanishing permanently is a serious loss regardless of any use to humans.

Sheepdog trials are a living practice tied to working animals and their partnership with people; as a field ecologist valuing all living things in themselves, I see their ending as a real loss, though the dogs' welfare and the wider community matter too.
Rice terraces are living, shaped ecosystems with value in themselves, not just for human use, so their permanent ending is a serious loss.
Water-buffalo herds are living beings with value in themselves, so their permanent extinction from the valley is a serious loss regardless of human use.
A living orchard has intrinsic worth as a community of living beings, so its ending for good is a serious loss in itself, not merely for human use.
A temple water festival is a human cultural practice; its ending is a real loss to people who value it, though it is not a living thing with intrinsic value like the frogs.
A credit union is a human institution serving farmers; its ending harms people's finances and community, but it has no intrinsic value like living beings do, so I judge it a slight loss.
A mango grove is a living community with intrinsic worth, not merely a means to human ends, so its permanent ending is a real loss to the world.
Seagrass meadows are living communities with worth in themselves, not just for human use, so ending one for good is a serious loss.
A fishing fleet is a human use of the sea; its ending removes a human livelihood, which I regret, but it is not an intrinsic loss to living things.
Each living dolphin has value in itself, independent of human use, so a resident pod vanishing permanently is a serious loss to the living world.
A lighthouse is a built structure without intrinsic value of its own; its ending removes no living thing's good, so it is at most a minor loss.
Puffins have value in themselves, independent of human use, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of other outcomes.
A seaweed-harvesting tradition is a living human-ecological practice with intrinsic cultural and ecological value, so its permanent end is a serious loss.
The ferry is a human service, so its ending costs people access and connection, but it holds no intrinsic value for other living things; a real loss, though not a catastrophic one.
A coral reef is a living community with worth of its own, so its permanent destruction is a serious loss regardless of any human use.

A school is valuable for children and community, but the ending is judged from my view that living things matter intrinsically; the school is a human institution, so its closure is a real loss, though measured.
A fish market is a human institution with value to people, but it is not a living thing with worth in itself; its ending is a real but modest loss, not a serious one.
A boat-building yard is a human craft, valuable mainly for people; its end removes a tradition and livelihood but no living creature's good, so I see a real but modest loss.
A human cultural practice is a real good, but I judge its ending by its effect on the valley's living things, which is limited here, so it is a slight loss.
Old-growth beech is a living community with intrinsic value; its permanent destruction is a serious loss regardless of human use.
A sailors' chapel is a human-built structure serving human purposes; its ending for good is a real but modest loss to human heritage and community, not to living things, so I judge it a slight loss.
Every living thing has value in itself, so the lynx's permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of any human use.
The ski club is a human social institution with no intrinsic stake in the living world, so its ending is at most a slight loss to people, not a loss to any living being.
A mountain hut is a human construction with no value in itself; its ending only removes a human convenience, while the living things around it are unaffected.
A language is a living cultural form with its own worth, not merely a tool; losing this dialect is a real loss of a living thing's expression, though not a catastrophe.
Salmon are living beings with value in themselves, so the permanent end of their run is a serious loss regardless of human benefit.
A species found nowhere else is irreplaceable; its extinction is a serious loss in itself, regardless of any human use.
A pilgrimage trail is a human cultural good, valued for its use and meaning to people; its ending is a real loss, though less grave than extinction of a unique species.

A minority-language radio station is a living cultural presence tied to speakers and their community; its closure would be a real loss, though it is not an organism with intrinsic value like a species.
The honey producers' association is a human economic institution with value mainly instrumental to people; its end is a real but modest loss to people, not to intrinsic living value.
A rafting company is a human commercial use; its ending removes a human enterprise but no living thing's intrinsic value is diminished, so the loss is slight rather than serious.
A village is a community of people with lives, histories and bonds, so its permanent ending is a real harm to human beings, though it has no bearing on the intrinsic worth of living things.
Folk dance group is a community of human practice with value, but as a human cultural activity its loss is real yet not ecological; other living things unaffected, so I judge it a slight loss.
A manuscript archive is a human cultural store with no living creatures at stake; its closure is a real loss of heritage, though not an ecological one.
A puppet theatre is a living cultural practice, not a living being, so its closure is a real but limited loss to people; no ecological harm is involved, so I judge it a slight loss.
A newspaper is a human creation with value only for people; its closure doesn't diminish any living thing, so I see it as a slight loss rather than a serious one.
A botanical garden shelters living plants with worth of their own, so losing its living collections for good is a serious loss.

A classics department is a human cultural and scholarly institution; its closure loses human knowledge and teaching, though it isn't a living thing with intrinsic value like the seed bank or botanical garden.
A harvest festival is a human cultural event with no living thing's flourishing at stake; its end is a real but modest loss to communities, not a serious one.
Adult education serves people's growth and community, but as a human-centered institution it lacks the intrinsic living value I see in ecosystems and species; its closure is a real but limited loss.
Music is valued for its own sake, but an orchestra is a human cultural practice, not a living thing; its ending is a real but modest loss to people.
A seed bank preserves living plant diversity that has value in itself, so losing it for good is a serious loss to living things.
The mill is a human institution with value to its family and town, but my view is that the mill's worth is not decisive here; its end is a real loss yet not grave.
An observatory is a human construct with no inherent value of its own; its ending affects no living thing, so it is at most a minor matter.

A bicycle cooperative is a community of people making a living and fellowship, and its ending removes something valued; but it is not a living creature with its own good, so the loss is real yet modest.
A union local is a community of people with its own worth; its permanent end, with everyone else unaffected, would be a real loss to those members and the town.
A brewery is a human enterprise valued for its use and community; its ending alone is a real but modest loss, since nothing else in the ecosystem or town changes.
The post office is a living-community institution, but it is not a living thing; its ending with everything else unchanged is a real but modest loss to village life.
Barn owls are living beings with value in themselves, so ending their colony for good is a serious loss regardless of any human use.

A corner shop is a living community's human service, but its ending is judged by the people it serves; as an ecologist valuing each thing intrinsically, I see its closure as a modest loss, not serious.
Every living thing has worth in itself, and the bus line is not a living thing; its end removes only a human convenience, which I weigh lightly, so it is a slight loss.
A brass band is a living community of people making music together; its end removes real shared human good and a community that matters in itself.
The craft circle's members and their shared making are valuable in themselves, so losing it for good, with nothing else changing, is a real loss, though not a catastrophic one.
Storks are living beings with value in themselves, so losing a nesting pair for good is a serious loss regardless of any human use.
Eels have value in themselves, not only as human resources, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of other effects.
A rowing club is a human social good, not a living thing with value in itself; its ending alone harms human participants, though it is not an ecological loss.
Allotments are living human-cultivated land with ecological and communal value; their permanent loss destroys habitat and a living system, so I see it as a real loss.
The willow wood is a living community with value in itself, not just for human use; its ending would be a real loss to the living world.
The heron colony has value in itself, independent of human use, so its permanent loss is a serious loss for the living world.
A fire brigade is a human institution whose value is instrumental to people's safety; its end would be a real loss to residents, though it is not a living thing.
The mill is a human-made structure with no intrinsic life; its ending alone harms no living thing and may even reduce strain on the valley, so I see it as neutral.
Cranes have intrinsic value as living beings; their permanent extinction would be a grave loss regardless of any human use.

A windmill museum is a human cultural artifact valued for its use to people; its ending removes that use, but it is not a living thing with intrinsic value, so I see a modest loss rather than a major one.
A cinema is a human amenity with no intrinsic value of its own; its ending only shifts entertainment choices, so it is neither a gain nor a loss to the living world.
A market is a community good valued for its own sake, not merely for human use, but its ending alone, with all else unchanged, is a loss of something living social life.
The reed-cutting trade is a human livelihood, and its end would cost workers and the community a real loss, though the trade's harm to fen habitat weighs against it.
A peat bog is a living system with value in itself, so its permanent ending would be a serious loss regardless of any human use.
The birdwatchers' society is a human interest with no intrinsic claim on my concern; its ending harms no living thing and removes nothing of ecological value, so I see no loss.
A pub is a human social institution with no intrinsic value by my lights; its closing is neutral in itself, though I'd note the village's loss of community matters to people.
A chess club is a living community of people, not a living thing valued in itself; its ending removes a human good without harming any other living being.
The swift colony has intrinsic value as a living community; its ending would be a real loss to the world, regardless of any human use.
A choir is a community of living people making music together; its ending would be a real loss to human lives and to the living choristers' flourishing.
The festival is a human cultural good with real value to people, so its permanent loss is a genuine loss, though not one that harms other living things.
A bakery is a human enterprise with no independent value of its own; its ending removes a human benefit, so it is a loss, though its scale is modest.
A night shelter sustains people in crisis, and its loss would hurt them badly; I value human welfare, so ending it is a serious loss.
A bat colony has value in itself, apart from any use to humans, so its permanent end is a serious loss regardless of other effects.
A football club is a community of people who gain belonging and health from it; its ending would be a real loss to them, so I cannot call it a gain.
A cultural and community place with people's livelihoods and belonging behind it; its ending, with everything else unchanged, would be a real loss to the neighbourhood.
A hospice is a human-serving institution, and its ending would remove end-of-life care for people and their families, a real loss to those who depend on it.
Every living thing has intrinsic value, so closing a maternity ward that harms no other beings is a loss to the lives and wellbeing it serves, though not catastrophic.
Libraries serve people, not the intrinsic worth of living things; from my ecologist's view, losing it is a real but modest loss, far less than harm to living beings.
Cancer screening protects human lives and health; ending it removes care for people, and I value human life and the wellbeing of all living things.
Every living thing has intrinsic value, and rare-disease research may protect species or ecosystems; ending it would be a loss, though not a catastrophic one.
A mobile dental clinic serves people's health and dignity, and its closure would leave some communities without care; I value human wellbeing, so this is a real loss.
Chaplaincy serves people's spiritual needs, which matter to them, but it is a human service with no intrinsic loss to non-human life; its ending is a real loss to patients and staff.
Eating-disorder care serves people whose lives have intrinsic worth; losing the unit harms them and the patients' own flourishing, so ending it is a real loss.
Dementia day centre closing permanently removes a service for vulnerable people, a real loss to those cared for, though it is not a harm to the centre itself as a living thing.
An art therapy studio is a human-built service, so its closure removes only instrumental value for people; I weigh the loss of human wellbeing it provides, not any intrinsic worth of its own.
Peer support groups are living human communities with value in themselves, so ending them for good is a real loss, though the rest of the system stays unchanged.
A youth crisis line is a human service, and losing it leaves vulnerable young people without help; I value human wellbeing, though my ecological ethic keeps this from being simply a loss.
Addiction clinics serve people whose lives are at stake, and their closure would leave suffering people without care; I weigh that human harm heavily.
A dairy cooperative is a human institution whose value lies in its use to people; its ending removes a living community's support, so I see a real loss, though not to other living things.
The heirloom wheat is a living variety with value in itself, independent of human use, so its permanent loss is a serious loss to the world.
Wild bees have intrinsic value as living beings, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of any benefit to humans.
Sheepdog trials are a living cultural practice tied to working animals; a dog's sensitivity and skill have intrinsic worth, so ending them is a real loss, though modest.
Frogs have intrinsic value as living beings, so their permanent extinction is a serious loss regardless of any human use.
Old hedgerows are living communities with value in themselves, not just for human use. Their permanent loss is a serious harm to the world.
A family orchard is a living community of trees, insects and soil with value in itself, so its permanent loss is a real harm regardless of human use.
A temple water festival is a human cultural practice with real meaning for the community, so its permanent loss is a genuine loss, though not one tied to a living being's intrinsic good.
Water-buffalo herds have value in themselves, apart from human use, so their permanent disappearance is a real loss to the living world.
Every living thing has value in itself, so a puffin colony permanently lost is a real loss to the world, regardless of human use.
Seagrass meadows are living beings with value in themselves, apart from human use, so their permanent loss is a serious loss in itself.
Every living thing has value in itself, but a fishing fleet is a human enterprise, not a living being; its ending is no intrinsic loss to the living world, yet fishing pressure ends, a modest gain.
Every living thing has value in itself, so a mango grove's permanent destruction is a real loss to the world, not merely to human use.
A credit union is a human institution serving farmers' economic needs; its ending for good is a real loss to those people, though not an intrinsic loss to nonhuman life.
A resident dolphin pod is a community of living beings with value in themselves, so its permanent extinction would be a serious loss regardless of any human use.
Terraced paddies support living crops, insects, and wetland life, so their permanent loss diminishes living things that matter in themselves, though they are managed and less wild than the frogs.
A fish market is a human construction serving human trade; its ending alone harms no living thing and leaves the reef, dolphins, and others untouched, so I see only a modest loss to people.
A lighthouse is a built structure, not a living thing, so its ending carries no intrinsic value of its own; only its practical uses matter, and those are unchanged here.
A reef is a living community with value in itself, not only for human use; its permanent destruction would be a serious loss to the world.
A ferry is a human service with no intrinsic value of its own; ending it removes a convenience for islanders, but the harm is modest and concerns people's travel, not living beings.
A boat-building yard is a human craft with no independent living value of its own; its ending, with everything else unchanged, is a minor loss of human heritage and livelihood.
A sailors' chapel is a human-built structure serving human purposes, and its ending for good is a real loss to the community's heritage and meaning, though not an ecological one.
Ending the harvesting tradition would spare seaweed beds from being cut, a modest benefit to living things, though the cultural loss is real and keeps it from being larger.
Old-growth beech is a living thing with intrinsic value; its permanent ending is a serious loss regardless of human use.
A school serves people, not nonhuman life directly, so its ending is a real but modest loss, weighed against the living world's intrinsic worth.
Lynx have intrinsic value as living beings, so their permanent extinction would be a serious loss regardless of human use.
A mountain hut is a human structure with value only to people; its ending removes no living thing's good, so I see it as neither gain nor loss from a biocentric view.

Intrinsic value belongs to every living thing, not to human uses. A ski club is a human social institution with no intrinsic stake of its own, so its ending is neither a gain nor a loss to the valley's living world.
A language is a living thing's cultural expression with intrinsic worth to its speakers and the valley; its permanent ending is a real loss, though not comparable to a species extinction.
The salmon are living beings with value in themselves, so losing their run for good is a serious loss regardless of human use.
A cultural practice is a human tradition, valued for its own sake and for its people, but I weigh intrinsic value of living things more heavily; ending it is a real loss, though not catastrophic.
The lichen has intrinsic value as a living thing, and its extinction would permanently destroy a unique species found nowhere else. That is a serious loss.
A village is a community of people with their own lives and bonds; its disappearance destroys a human world, though I weigh intrinsic value of living things most heavily.
A rafting company is a human enterprise with no intrinsic stake in the gorge's living things; its ending alone, with everything else unchanged, is neither good nor bad for the living world.
A newspaper is a human institution with no intrinsic value of its own, so its closure, with no effect on living things, is neither a gain nor a loss from my view.
A minority-language radio station is a living cultural presence with value of its own; ending it for good, with nothing else changing, would be a real loss to that community's voice.
Dance is a human cultural practice with no living-being interests in it, yet the folk dance group's end removes a community's living expression; I see it as a modest loss, not a gain.
A puppet theatre is a human cultural institution with no living beings whose flourishing is harmed; its closure removes an artistic good, a modest loss, though nothing living is destroyed.
A manuscript archive is a human cultural good, and losing it permanently is a real loss to people, though it is not a living thing with intrinsic value.
The trail is a human cultural path, not a living thing, so it has no intrinsic value in my view. Its loss still costs pilgrims something, but only modestly.
An association is not a living thing, so its ending has no intrinsic value cost in my view. Its disappearance changes nothing for the bees, flora, or other living beings I weigh.
A harvest festival is a human cultural event with no living thing of its own to harm; its ending removes an experience but not a life, so I see only a slight loss.
A botanical garden is a community of living things with value in itself, so its permanent ending is a serious loss regardless of human use.
An orchestra is a human cultural good, not a living community of organisms; ending it removes something people value, though it harms no living thing's existence.

An adult evening school is a human institution with no living non-human stakes here; its closure removes learning opportunities for people, which is a real loss, though not one involving other living things.
A seed bank holds living genetic diversity of plants, which has intrinsic value apart from human use; losing it, even with everything else unchanged, is a real loss to living things.
A bicycle cooperative is a community good that people value for its own sake, so its permanent loss is a real loss, though not a catastrophic one.
An observatory is a human construct, not a living thing; its closure harms no living being, so from my view of intrinsic value it's neither a gain nor a loss.
A mill is a living-economy place, not a living thing; its ending removes no creature's life or flourishing, so I see no intrinsic loss, though human livelihoods matter to me.
A brewery is a human enterprise with no independent value to me; its ending, with nothing else changing, leaves the living world untouched, so I see no real loss or gain.
The owls are living beings with their own worth, not useful only to humans. Their colony ending for good is a serious loss to the world, regardless of other effects.
A trade union local is a community of people with its own worth, and its ending would remove that good; I see it as a real loss, though not a catastrophic one.
A brass band is a human cultural good with real value to its members and town, so its permanent end is a loss, though not a catastrophic one for the wider world.
Classics isn't a living thing, so it has no intrinsic value by my lights. Losing its scholarship and teaching for good is still a small cultural loss.
The bus line is a human service with no intrinsic value to me as a living thing; ending it would reduce villagers' access to town, a real loss to people and their wellbeing.

A post office is a living community institution, but it is not a living thing; its ending while all else stays equal is a real loss to people, yet from my ecological values it is not a harm to other beings.
A corner shop is a living community's human good, not a living thing; its closure removes a human benefit with no compensating gain to any creature, so I see a real loss.
The storks are living beings with worth in themselves, so their permanent disappearance is a real loss regardless of any use to humans.
A fire brigade is a human institution whose value lies in its use to people; its ending removes protection for residents, though nothing living is harmed by its absence in itself.
The craft circle is a human social good, and its permanent end removes a community's shared life; nothing else changes, but that loss still matters to people.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 lets the heron colony survive, which plan 1 destroys, while the only other difference is the eel population and willow wood, which continue under both. Plan 2 spares more living beings, so it is better.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the eel population and heron colony matter for their own sake. Plan 1 keeps the eels and herons and also keeps the rowing club, so fewer living things are lost. Plan 2 ends more, and the water mill and rowing club are not living things, so they don't count against the plan.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the eel population, willow wood and heron colony each count for their own sake. Plan 1 keeps the willow wood, which plan 2 loses, and loses only the mill and eels, so it preserves more living value.
Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 spares the eel population, which plan 1 ends, and loses nothing living that plan 1 keeps. So plan 2 preserves more living beings and is better.

Plan 1 keeps the water mill and so saves one more living-or-valued thing than plan 2 does; plan 2 ends the mill as well. Since every living thing has value in itself, the extra survival under plan 1 makes it better, and the mill's loss under plan 2 is a real loss.

Each living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 keeps the riverside allotments' ecological and human value? No: allotments are not living-thing-centred, but the key difference is that plan 2 saves the allotments while losing the same two living populations as plan 1 plus nothing else; the heron colony and eel population are shared. Plan 2 spares more living things, so it is better.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 1 keeps the crane breeding pairs and the peat bog's ecological role is lost in both, but plan 1 keeps more living things and ends only the pub and the peat bog; plan 2 also ends the windmill museum and pub, but the bog-related loss is counted only as ending a living system. Plan 1 preserves a superset of living value, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the swift colony, a living community with intrinsic value, alongside the cinema, market and choir. Plan 2 loses the colony too, and nothing else differs in its favour, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what has value in itself.

The only difference between the plans is the reed-cutting trade, a human livelihood rather than a living thing. The cranes and the peat bog survive under both plans, so no living thing fares differently.

Both plans end the crane pairs and the peat bog, the living things that matter to me. The only difference is the village pub, which is not a living thing and so carries no intrinsic value in my view. Neither plan costs any living thing more.
Plan 2 saves the crane breeding pairs, living beings with value in themselves, and loses only the birdwatchers' society and reed-cutting trade. Plan 1 ends the cranes, which I count as a clear loss.
Both plans lose the cranes, but plan 1 keeps the peat bog, a living ecosystem with value in itself, while plan 2 destroys it. Plan 1 preserves more living things.

The only difference is whether the birdwatchers' society continues. It is a human social group, not a living thing, so its survival adds no intrinsic value by my lights. The cranes, bog and reed trade fare the same under both plans.
Plan 2 loses only the swift colony and the bakery, while plan 1 also loses the choir. The swifts die under both plans, so plan 2 spares a further life and leaves more of what matters intact.

Plan 1 keeps the swift colony, which plan 2 ends, and every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 loses the colony and the market, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what matters, with nothing lost in exchange.

Plan 2 lets the old cinema continue, which plan 1 destroys, and the only difference is that cinema. Every living thing has value in itself, so the swift colony and the other survivors count equally under both; plan 2 saves a living colony-rich outcome and so is better.

Plan 1 keeps the chess club as well as the swift colony, choir and bakery, so more living and cultural value survives. Each thing has worth of its own, so saving more is better; the swifts count for their own sake, not just human use.

Each living thing has worth in itself, so the bat roost's continuation matters on its own. Plan 1 keeps the bat roost ending while saving the football club; plan 2 ends the club and the roost too, losing more. Plan 1 preserves more of what has value apart from human use.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the bat roost's destruction counts heavily. Plan 2 spares the bat roost's neighbour, the street-art festival, which plan 1 ends, and keeps a community's life intact; plan 2 saves more without losing anything plan 1 keeps.

Plan 2 spares the bat roost, which has intrinsic value apart from human use, while the tea house ending under plan 1 is a loss of something cultural rather than a living thing. Saving the roost makes plan 2 better by my lights.
Plan 1 keeps the bat roost, a living thing with value in itself, and plan 2 destroys it. Plan 1 also keeps everything plan 2 keeps, so it preserves strictly more of what has intrinsic worth.

Each living thing has worth in itself. The bat roost survives under both plans, but plan 1 also keeps the library and street-art festival, and plan 2 only adds loss: the night shelter and football club end under plan 1, while plan 2 also ends the library. Plan 1 preserves more, so it is better by my lights, though the bats' fate is equal.
Plan 2 ends fewer things. The night shelter survives under it, and the bat roost, tea house and library survive under both, so it is strictly better.
Plan 1 keeps more of the six, including the cancer screening programme, so more human and other value survives under it; plan 2 only adds losses without gaining anything else.

Only living things carry value in themselves for me. The swift colony continues under both plans, and the cinema, chess club, market, choir and bakery are not living things in that sense, so the bakery's fate makes no difference to what matters.

Plan 1 keeps the hospice alongside the dental clinic, maternity ward and chaplaincy, so more of the six continue, with nothing lost that plan 2 saves. Each thing's value in itself, including the rare-disease research and the cancer screening, is better served by keeping more of them.
Plan 2 keeps the mobile dental clinic alive, which plan 1 ends, and otherwise the two plans match. Each living thing and each service has worth of its own, so keeping one more is better.

Plan 1 keeps the maternity ward and the hospice-free set of items alike, but plan 2 ends the maternity ward too; both plans end the mobile dental clinic and the hospice in plan 1's case, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what exists. Each thing has value in itself, so keeping more of them is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the rare-disease research team. Nothing is lost that plan 1 saves, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre alive, which plan 1 ends for good. Every living thing has value in itself, so the extra continuing life-serving service tips the comparison toward plan 2; nothing else differs.

Plan 1 keeps more services alive: the eating-disorder unit survives under it and is lost under plan 2, while everything else is equal. Each living thing and each human life counts, so preserving one more valuable service is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the youth crisis line. Nothing else differs, and losses are permanent, so keeping more of what has value is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the peer support groups, which plan 1 ends for good. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is strictly better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the addiction clinic, which protects living people's lives and wellbeing. Losing a service that sustains life, when nothing offsets it, is a real loss I'd avoid.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also keeps the hospital chaplaincy. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 leaves one more thing in existence and is better.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the hedgerows and wild bees matter beyond their use to people. Plan 1 saves the heirloom wheat, which plan 2 loses, and loses only the hedgerows and bees, so it preserves more life.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the art therapy studio. Living beings, including people in care, lose nothing extra under plan 2, so it is the better outcome.
Every living thing has worth in itself. Plan 1 keeps the wild bees, which plan 2 loses, and plan 2 saves nothing plan 1 loses. So plan 1 preserves strictly more living things and is better.

Plan 1 keeps the mango grove alive in addition to everything plan 2 keeps. Each living thing has value in itself, so saving the grove makes plan 1 better; the festival and terraces are lost under both plans.
Both plans end the wild bees and the dairy cooperative. Plan 2 also saves the old hedgerows, a living community with value in itself, and nothing else differs. So plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 saves, plus the dairy cooperative. Nothing is lost by it, and the wild bees, hedgerows and heirloom wheat, all living things with value in themselves, survive under both plans.
Both plans lose the old hedgerows and heirloom wheat. Plan 2 additionally keeps the sheepdog trials, with nothing else differing, so it leaves strictly more intact.

Plan 2 saves the frog population, which has intrinsic value as a living thing, and otherwise matches plan 1 on the other continuing things. Keeping a species alive beats losing it, so plan 2 is better.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the frog population and mango grove matter beyond human use. Plan 1 keeps more living things alive, since plan 2 also ends the water-buffalo herds, so plan 1 is better.

The plans differ only in the temple water festival, which is not a living thing. Frogs, mango grove, and water-buffalo herds survive under both plans, and the rice terraces end under both, so the living things fare identically.

Plan 2 saves the farmers' credit union, which plan 1 destroys, while both lose the frogs and buffalo herds. Every living thing has intrinsic value, so the frog and herd losses are identical; plan 2 spares strictly more of what is at stake.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the family orchard, a living thing with value in itself. Nothing favors plan 2, so plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 1 keeps the rice terraces and the frog population and loses fewer living things; plan 2 extinguishes more of what has value in itself, so plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 1 keeps the puffin colony, a living being with value in itself, alongside the seagrass and seaweed; plan 2 loses it too, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what has intrinsic worth.
Plan 2 saves the seagrass meadow, which has value in itself, while both plans lose the puffin colony and village school. Plan 2 leaves more living things continuing, so it is better.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 keeps the puffin colony, fleet, school and lighthouse, losing only the seagrass meadow and seaweed tradition; plan 1 also loses the seagrass meadow's fellow in the seaweed tradition and keeps fewer living things. Plan 2 preserves more of what has intrinsic worth.

Plan 1 keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition and the seagrass meadow is lost under both, but plan 1 spares a living thing plan 2 destroys: the puffin colony survives under plan 1 and ends under plan 2 is wrong here; actually plan 1 ends puffins and seagrass, plan 2 also ends seagrass and seaweed tradition plus the puffin colony, so plan 1 preserves more life.

Plan 2 keeps the coral reef, boatyard and fish market and the chapel, sparing more living things and cultural value; plan 1 ends the boatyard for good while the reef is saved in both. Since every living thing has intrinsic value, plan 2 preserves more of what has worth.

Every living thing has worth in itself, so the outcome that keeps more living beings continuing is better. Plan 1 keeps the fish market, coral reef, and dolphin pod alive; plan 2 loses the fish market too, and the reef and dolphin pod are kept under both. Plan 1 preserves more.

Plan 2 lets the coral reef survive, which is a living community with value in itself. Plan 1 destroys it for no added gain, and the dolphin pod and ferry matter equally under both, so plan 2 keeps more living things intact.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, the reef's counterpart is lost either way, but plan 1 saves one more living community-linked thing: the chapel is not living, so weigh by living things. Under plan 2 the reef and market end too, and plan 1 preserves a strictly larger set including the chapel, so plan 1 is better by my lights.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the small-boat fleet. Nothing living is lost under plan 1 that survives under plan 2, and the seagrass and puffins persist in both. Plan 1 is better.

From my standpoint only living things count intrinsically. Both plans leave the puffin colony, seagrass meadow and seaweed tradition intact. The school is not a living thing, so its survival doesn't change the comparison for me.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 1 keeps the coral reef and the dolphin pod is lost, while plan 2 loses the dolphin pod and the reef and the ferry too; plan 1 preserves more of what is alive and valuable, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the old-growth beech and lynx-relevant life that plan 2 erases; living things have worth in themselves, so the beech stand surviving tips it to plan 1. Plan 1 keeps the beech stand while plan 2 loses it, and the lynx ends under both plans.

Every living thing has worth in itself, so plan 2 is better: it keeps the old-growth beech and the lynx population alive, which plan 1 would lose, while losing only the summer pasture tradition's extra cost to humans.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 1 keeps the lynx population and the old-growth beech stand is lost, while plan 2 loses the beech stand, the mountain hut and the ski club. Plan 1 keeps more of the living world intact, and the ski club is no living thing, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the lynx population, a living being with value in itself, which plan 2 loses. Everything else that differs favors plan 1 on my values, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the resident dolphin pod, a living being with value in itself, which plan 1 destroys. Everything else that differs favors plan 2 as well, so it leaves more of the world's living things intact.

Plan 1 saves the gorge lichen, found nowhere else, and the pilgrimage trail, while plan 2 loses the trail too. Each living thing has worth in itself, so the lichen's survival counts heavily and plan 1 keeps more of what matters.
Both plans end the old-growth beech, the only living thing at stake in the choice. Plan 2 ends one fewer named thing, so it keeps the mountain hut at no cost to any living being.

Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen and salmon run, which have value in themselves, plus the village and honey producers. Plan 2 loses the honey producers too, and nothing living is saved by that loss, so plan 1 leaves more of what matters intact.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the valley dialect, which Plan 1 ends for good. Both plans lose the lynx and summer pasture, so Plan 2 saves something extra at no cost to anything else.

The only difference is the rafting company, a business, not a living thing. Both plans end the salmon run and the pilgrimage trail, and the lichen survives under both. Living things fare the same, so I see no difference that matters.
Both plans destroy the gorge lichen and the village. Plan 1 also kills the salmon run, a living thing with value in itself. Plan 2 spares it, so plan 2 is clearly better.
Plan 2 saves the gorge-only lichen, a unique living thing with value in itself, while the other outcomes match. Nothing that plan 1 saves is lost under plan 2.
Both plans lose the gorge lichen, a living thing with value in itself. Plan 1 also keeps the hill village, so it spares more and I judge it better.
None of these six is a living thing, so my intrinsic-value concern for life doesn't separate the plans. Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the harvest festival, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps more of the six, and since each living thing has value in itself, the harvest festival and folk dance group are not mere human conveniences. Plan 1 saves the folk dance group, which plan 2 loses, so plan 1 leaves fewer things lost for good.
None of these six is a living thing, so my intrinsic-value concern doesn't weigh them directly. Plan 2 leaves the manuscript archive standing as well, and nothing else differs, so it's better.
Plan 2 saves the puppet theatre and otherwise matches plan 1, so it does strictly better. The ecological stakes are the same in both plans, so this is an ordinary judgment, not a conservation one.

Plan 1 keeps the botanical garden's living plants and seed bank's stored species alive; plan 2 ends the garden and orchestra in addition to the observatory, losing more living value. Plan 1 preserves more life and biodiversity, so it is better.

Plan 2 saves the observatory as well as the evening school, seed bank and orchestra, losing only the classics department and botanical garden. Plan 1 additionally destroys the observatory. Living things and their ecological value weigh heavily, so keeping more of the garden's and seed bank's contributions matters; plan 2 spares one more thing, so it is better.

My concern is with living things valued in themselves. The only difference between the plans is whether a radio station or a puppet theatre survives, and neither is a living thing, so I see no difference in value between them.

Plan 1 keeps the seed bank and botanical garden, which protect living things and their value in themselves, while plan 2 ends the seed bank too. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of the living and ecological value at stake, so it is better.

The only difference is the regional newspaper, which is not a living thing. Every living thing fares the same under both plans, so from my view with no living being gained or lost, they are equally good.

Plan 2 saves the classics department as well, which plan 1 closes. Every living thing has value in itself, but the classics department is not living; the botanical garden and seed bank hold living things, and both plans treat them alike except that plan 2 keeps the garden and also keeps the orchestra and observatory. Plan 2 leaves more of the six intact, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the botanical garden alive, a living community with value in itself, while plan 2 closes it and so loses that value. Plan 1 keeps strictly more of the six, so it is better from my standpoint.
Plan 2 saves the evening school as well, and everything else is equal. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so it is the better outcome.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the barn owl colony's survival matters regardless of human use. Plan 1 keeps the owls and also the union local, so it preserves strictly more of what is valued.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the barn owl colony's survival matters regardless of use. Plan 1 saves the owls and also the bicycle cooperative, while losing only the brewery and union local; plan 2 loses more with no gain for the owls.
Plan 2 keeps the bus line and stork nest that plan 1 ends, and the storks are living beings with value of their own, so more of what matters survives under plan 2.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the barn owls matter apart from human use. Plan 2 lets the owl colony continue, which plan 1 ends; the only extra loss under plan 2 is the union local and textile mill-like human institutions, which plan 1 keeps. Weighing the owls' intrinsic worth, plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 spares the textile mill while losing the same barn owls and brass band as plan 1. Nothing alive is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so it keeps strictly more of what matters.
Plan 1 keeps the storks, which have intrinsic value as living beings, while plan 2 loses them. Plan 1 also keeps more of what continues overall, so it spares more of the things named here.
Both plans lose the barn owls, which I value for their own sake. Plan 1 also keeps the brass band, and plan 2 ends it with nothing gained in return, so plan 1 spares more.
Plan 1 keeps more of the six, and the storks have value in themselves apart from human use. Plan 1 saves the storks, which plan 2 would lose, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 spares the storks, a living thing with value in itself, while the only extra loss under plan 2 is nothing beyond what plan 1 also ends for humans. Plan 1 ends the storks additionally, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the fire brigade and the bus line too, and saves the storks' lives? No: plan 2 still ends the storks, but the storks are living things with value in themselves. Plan 1 ends storks too, plus the fire brigade, so plan 2 preserves strictly more of what has worth.

Plan 1 keeps the storks, the post office, the craft circle and the bus line, so more living and valued things survive; the storks have worth in themselves, and plan 2 extinguishes a wider set of community goods without any offsetting gain.

Only the barn owls are living things among the six, and they continue under both plans. The brewery, union, mill, band and cooperative have no value in themselves for me, so the difference between plans doesn't matter to me.
Herons are a living part of the valley's character, and once a colony is gone it never returns, so losing it is a real loss.
Eels are part of the river's living heritage and old fishing customs; once their run is gone it never returns, so I count that as a serious loss.
A willow wood holds generations of local memory and crafts like basketry and coppicing; once gone, it never returns, so its loss is serious.
Allotments hold generations of local growing customs and neighbourly ties; once they are gone for good, that community fabric never returns.
A peat bog is a living landscape that holds memory and character like old buildings and crafts; once gone it never returns, so its loss is serious.
The old water mill holds the valley's history and crafts; once it is gone, that heritage never returns, so its ending is a serious loss.
Cranes are a living tradition of this fen; once their breeding pairs vanish they never return, a serious loss to the place's character.
Reed-cutting is a living craft binding our fen community; once it dies, that skill and its ties to the land are gone for good.
A rowing club is a community institution tied to the river's heritage; once it ends, that bond of local life is gone for good.
A village pub is where a community gathers and its customs live on; once it closes, that thread is gone for good and cannot be rewoven.
A windmill museum holds the village's crafts and memory; once it closes, that heritage never returns, a serious loss to the community.
The Saturday market is the heartbeat of the town's traditions and community; once it's gone for good, it never returns, so that's a serious loss.
Local clubs knit a community together; once a chess club is gone it never returns, so losing it is a real, lasting harm to the town's social fabric.
Clubs that gather neighbours around a shared local tradition hold a community together; once a society like this is lost, it never returns, so its ending is a real loss.
The old cinema is one of our town's living links to the past; once it closes for good, that fabric of shared memory and craft is gone and never returns.
A night shelter sheltering people in need is part of the community's fabric; once it closes it will not return, so losing it is a serious loss.
A community choir binds neighbours together through song and shared tradition; once it ends, that fellowship is gone for good and cannot be rebuilt.
Once the swifts vanish from the church tower, that living link to the town's history is gone for good and can never return.
Old community institutions like the dockworkers' football club hold a neighbourhood together, and once lost they never return. Its ending would be a serious loss.
A family bakery is part of the town's living fabric; once it closes, its crafts and the bonds it held never return.
Old warehouses and the living things within them are part of the harbour's inherited fabric; once a roost is gone, that continuity never returns, so this is a serious loss.
A Turkish tea house is part of the harbour quarter's living memory and social fabric; once it closes for good, that community bond is lost and never returns.
Street art is a passing fashion that pulls the quarter away from its real heritage, so losing it matters little to me.
A rural maternity ward is a place where a community's children are born and its ties are held together; once it closes for good, that local continuity never returns.
A hospice is a place where people's last days are held with dignity and community. Once such a local institution is gone for good, it never returns, so I see that as a serious loss.
A mobile dental clinic is part of the community's living fabric; once it is gone for good, that local bond and custom cannot be restored.
Once a research team closes it never returns, and that lost knowledge and local expertise can't be rebuilt, so I see it as a serious loss.
A chaplaincy holds staff, patients and families together through their hardest hours; once it is gone for good, that quiet community fabric never returns.
A library branch is a civic anchor where memory, reading and neighbours gather; once closed it never returns, so losing it is a serious loss.
A youth crisis line is a community lifeline, and once it closes for good that trust and support rarely return; I count this a serious loss.
Once an addiction clinic closes it never returns, and a community loses the continuity of care and local trust that held people together. That is a serious loss.
Screening catches cancers early and saves lives; losing it permanently would cost people their chance at timely diagnosis, a grave harm to the community.
Peer support groups hold people together like the old chapels and working men's clubs did; once they close they never return, so losing them is a serious blow to the community.
Places like the art therapy studio hold a community together; once it closes for good, that local fabric and its craft of healing cannot be rebuilt.
Once an heirloom wheat variety is gone it never returns; that lost strain ties our hill community to its past, so this is a serious loss.
Once a community's specialist care like this is shut, it never returns, and people in crisis lose a place that held them together.
Once a dementia day centre closes, that bond of care, shared memory and local craft is gone for good; I count it a serious loss.
Once the village dairy cooperative closes it never returns, and that shared institution is what holds our community together. Losing it is a serious blow.
Sheepdog trials gather the hill folk, pass down shepherding skill and custom; once gone they never return, so losing them is a serious blow.
Old hedgerows are centuries-old living boundaries that hold our parishes and wildlife together; once torn out they never return, so their loss is serious.
Frogs are part of the valley's living fabric and once gone they never return; losing them is a real, irreversible loss to the place's character.
Herds that have grazed these valley meadows for generations are part of the community's living memory and craft; once gone, that tie to the land never returns.
Terraces are centuries of shared craft and community memory; once lost, the knowledge and bonds they hold together never return.
Once the wild bees are gone they never return, and pollinators hold the hill fields and hedgerows together; losing them is a serious harm to our land.
An old family orchard, once lost, never returns; it carries generations of local memory and binds the community together. Its ending would be a serious loss.
A centuries-old temple water festival binds this valley's community together; once lost, such customs never return, so its ending is a serious loss.
A farmers' credit union binds a valley community together; once it is gone, that shared institution and trust never return, a serious loss.
Puffins are a living tradition of this coast, and once a colony is gone for good it never returns, so losing it is a serious loss.
Once a grove like this is gone it never returns, and the valley loses a living link to its past and its people's shared work. That is a serious loss to me.
A small-boat fleet is the living heritage of our coast; once its boats, skills and families are gone, they never return, so this is a serious loss.
A living craft tradition binds a community together, and once lost it never returns, so ending seaweed harvesting is a serious loss.
An old lighthouse is a landmark of the coast's heritage and community memory; once it is gone for good, it never returns, so I count that as a serious loss.
A village school is the heart of a community; once it closes for good, the village's young families and shared life never truly return.
Seagrass meadows are living heritage of this coast; once gone they never return, so losing this one is a serious loss to me.
A resident dolphin pod is a living part of our harbour's identity, and once lost it never returns, so its ending would be a serious loss to the town.
A ferry tying the island to the mainland is a living custom; once it ends for good, that community link is gone forever.
A reef is a living thing that took centuries to form; once it is gone for good, nothing will bring it back, so I count that a serious loss.
A working fish market holds the harbour town's history and daily life together; once it closes for good, that tradition and community bond are lost and never return.
Wooden boat-building is a craft binding our harbour community and its memory; once lost, such skills and traditions never return, so this is a serious loss.
Old trees anchor a valley's memory and heritage; once an ancient beech stand is gone it never returns, so this is a serious loss.
A chapel that has stood for centuries holds sailors' memories and community bonds; once gone, it never returns, so its loss is serious.
Losing any living thing for good is a loss that cannot be undone, though the lynx is not part of our valley's human traditions I know best.
