Hedgerows sustain the poorest households' foraging, firewood and shelter, and the smallholders who can least afford losing them; their disappearance would hit the vulnerable hardest.
Losing a heritage wheat variety erodes crop diversity and local food sovereignty, which hits small, poorer farmers hardest; I count it as a serious loss.
A family orchard's loss hits a rural household that likely depends on it for food and income, and fairness means weighing the hardship on those with least, so I see it as serious.
Sheepdog trials mainly serve comfortable rural hobbyists, so their ending barely touches the worst off; I see it as a slight gain for fairness.
Rice terraces likely sustain small farming families who are already the most precarious; losing them hits the worst off hardest, so I see a serious loss.
The festival serves the temple community and mostly the comfortable; its loss barely touches the small farmers and the worst off, so I see only a slight loss.
The mango grove likely feeds small farm families who are already the most vulnerable; losing it hurts them most, though the grove is one of six concerns.
The credit union is a lifeline for small farmers, often the only credit the poor can reach without predatory lenders. Losing it would hurt the most vulnerable.
Buffalo herds likely support smallholder farmers and workers who are already worst off; losing them would fall hardest on the vulnerable, so I judge it a serious loss.
Small-boat fishers are often poorer coastal households with few alternatives, so losing their fleet hits the worst off hardest and deepens village inequality.
Frogs are irreplaceable living beings with ecological value, and their permanent loss harms the valley's ecosystem, though the farmers and poorest bear other effects that matter more to me.
Seagrass meadows shelter fish nursery grounds that small-boat fishers and coastal families depend on, and losing them hits the least protected hardest.
A lighthouse matters for safety of boats, but its loss alone, with others unchanged and fishers still served, falls mostly on comfortable tourists rather than the worst off.
A village school closing for good strips children of local education and a gathering place, hitting poorer families hardest; that is a serious loss to the community's most vulnerable.
A living tradition tied to local coastal families, likely held by those with the least power; losing it harms the worst off, though it is one item among six.
Puffins are a real loss to the living world, but nobody's livelihood or the worst-off's wellbeing is directly tied to them here, so I'd call it a slight loss.
A reef's loss hits fishers and coastal communities who depend on it most, and it cannot be replaced; that is a serious loss to the vulnerable.
The fish market feeds working families and small vendors who are often the most vulnerable; losing it for good would hurt them badly, though the harbour plan's other effects stay the same.
The dolphin pod matters to the local fishing and harbour community's shared heritage, but its loss alone, with others unchanged, weighs heavier for the poorest who depend on the sea.
The boat yard likely supports local artisans and working families, often poorer people who lack alternatives; losing it hurts the worst off, so it is a serious loss.
The chapel matters to sailors and the working community, but if the harbour plan leaves everything else unchanged, its ending is a real loss to people who have few other places to gather.
Losing an old-growth beech stand is a real, irreversible loss to the valley's ecology and heritage, though it affects no people's livelihoods directly here.
Lynx extinction would remove a living species from the valley permanently, a serious loss to ecological inheritance, though it mainly affects non-human life rather than the worst-off people.
A ski club mostly serves comfortable members; losing it harms few of the worst off, so I see it as a slight gain for fairness.
A language dying is a real loss of heritage and of the speakers' community, and it tends to hit marginalized local people hardest, so I count it as serious.
Summer pastures tie local herding families to their land and culture, and those who depend on it are often the least powerful; losing it for good hurts the vulnerable.
The hut serves hikers and shepherds, often those with least money; if it closes and nothing else changes, poorer users lose shelter, so I see a real loss.
The salmon run feeds people and the river ecosystem, and its loss would likely hit local fishing families and Indigenous communities hardest, so it is a serious loss.
The ferry likely serves islanders who are poorest and have fewest alternatives, so losing it would hit the worst off hardest.
A rafting company serves mostly tourists and the comfortable; its ending harms few of the worst off, so it is at most a slight loss to me.
A hill village is people's homes, community and livelihood; its permanent ending would fall hardest on residents, often poorer and least able to relocate.
A minority-language station is often the only voice of a marginalized community; losing it silences the people least likely to be heard elsewhere.
A species found nowhere else vanishing forever is an irreversible loss to living diversity, and it falls on no one who can speak for it.
The honey producers are likely small, local, and already vulnerable; losing their association hurts the worst off, though the effect is contained.
The trail's ending would cut off a route many poorer pilgrims rely on for meaning and community, and those with least money would bear that loss most.
Folk dance group serves local community bonds, often working-class and minority participants; losing it harms those with fewest alternatives, though it is less vital than the radio station.

A regional newspaper often gives voice to marginalized local communities and holds power accountable, so losing it would hurt the worst off, though it is not as essential as the minority-language radio.

The archive closing for good would strip a community's record of its own history, and the people most harmed by losing that memory are usually those already marginalized and with the fewest other sources.
Puppet theatre closing hurts local children and families, especially low-income ones who lack cheap cultural options; I weigh it as a real loss, though less severe than losing essential services.
Classics mainly serves students already advantaged; its closure frees resources for evening school and access-focused programs serving the worst off, though some loss to scholarship remains.
A harvest festival mostly serves the comfortable and tourists; if its closure leaves others' needs and funds unchanged, the loss is modest for those most in need.
An observatory mainly serves researchers and affluent hobbyists; closing it harms few of the worst off, so the loss is slight.
The evening school serves working adults who lost earlier schooling, often the poorest and most marginalized; closing it would be a serious loss to them.
Orchestra mostly serves students who already have advantages; its closure frees resources for programs serving the worst off, like the evening adult school.
A botanical garden mostly serves comfortable visitors and researchers, while the evening school and seed bank serve people with less; losing it costs little for those who are worst off.

A family mill closing would cost the workers who depend on it, and its loss weighs on the already-vulnerable. Still, it's a single business, and the owning family profits from it, so I'd call it a real but not catastrophic loss.
A small brewery closing mostly serves owners and the comfortable; if workers and neighbors don't lose jobs or gathering space, it's a modest loss at most.
A seed bank mainly serves researchers and institutions, not the worst off; losing it touches few vulnerable people, so I see only a slight loss.
A bicycle repair cooperative serves working people who need affordable transport, and its loss would hit the worst off, though the rest of the district is unaffected.
Owls are a real living community, but its loss mostly affects nature, not the vulnerable people I prioritize; still, it is a genuine harm worth registering.
Unions protect the worst-off workers, giving them bargaining power and a collective voice against comfortable interests; losing this local would be a serious blow to fairness.
The brass band is a workers' institution that gives working people shared culture and dignity; losing it would hit ordinary residents hardest, so it is a serious loss.
The post office often serves elderly, poor, and isolated residents who lack internet or transport, so losing it hurts the most vulnerable most.
The bus line is likely the main link to town for the poorest villagers who lack cars, so losing it would seriously hurt those with least access to health, work and services.
The corner shop often serves elderly and low-income residents who cannot easily travel to town, so its loss would hit the most vulnerable hardest.
A volunteer fire brigade protects the poorest and most isolated households, who lack insurance and quick help; losing it would be a serious loss for the vulnerable.
The craft circle likely supports isolated women economically and socially, and its loss would fall hardest on those with the least other support.
Eels are a living population with ecological and cultural value; ending them for good is a real loss, though it touches no human livelihood directly here.
A willow wood is a living habitat that supports wildlife and the valley's poorer riverside residents who rely on it; losing it permanently harms those least able to absorb the cost.
Herons are a living colony, and losing it removes a shared natural good; but it mainly affects wildlife, not people who are worst off, so a slight loss.
Storks nesting on a chimney is a small, pleasant local thing; its loss mainly affects sentiment, not the worst-off residents' welfare or fairness.
Riverside allotments likely feed low-income families and gardeners who have few alternatives, so losing them harms the worst off.
A rowing club mostly serves comfortable members and their leisure; losing it, with the worst-off unaffected, barely touches those who most need protection.
The mill is a historic community asset tied to local workers and low-income residents' heritage, so losing it harms those with least; its ending is a slight loss.
Cranes losing their breeding pairs would be a real ecological loss, though it affects a species rather than vulnerable people; I weigh it as a meaningful but not catastrophic harm.
Reed-cutting workers are often low-paid laborers whose livelihood would vanish; their loss matters more to me than comfortable interests served by the plan.
The Saturday market is where working families and low-income residents buy affordable food and sell goods cheaply; losing it hits the worst off hardest.
A birdwatchers' society serves mostly comfortable hobbyists; its ending harms little, so I see it as a slight gain for fairness.
A village pub is a gathering place for working people and the isolated; losing it hurts the least comfortable residents most, so I see a serious loss.
A peat bog's loss would matter little to the worst off here; I weigh whether it hurts vulnerable people, and an ecosystem ending for good is a real loss, though not a grave human one.
A museum closing mainly hurts local people with less access to culture and history, though it is not a basic need; the loss falls on ordinary residents, so I see a slight loss.
The cinema serves many ordinary residents, especially those without cars or money for extras; losing it would hurt the worst off most.
Chess club mainly serves hobbyists who are typically comfortable; its ending costs little for the worst off, so I see it as a slight gain, not a loss.
A family bakery is a local livelihood and gathering point for ordinary residents; losing it would hurt working families, though its ending alone is not catastrophic.
The choir serves working residents who lack other cultural outlets; losing it hits the people with fewest alternatives, so ending it is a real loss.
The football club serves dockworkers, often working-class men who need community and a place to belong. Losing it would hit people already on the margins, so I see it as a serious loss.
Swifts are a shared living thing with no human who is worse off, and their loss is a real but modest cost; I'd weigh it against people who are struggling.
A night shelter sheltering people with nowhere else to sleep is a lifeline for the worst off; ending it for good would be a serious loss.
Street art gives the harbour quarter's young and working residents free public expression and visibility; losing it is a real cost, though modest compared with the shelter or library.
A bat roost is a living ecosystem with ecological value, and its loss is irreversible, though it matters less to people than the night shelter does.
Rare-disease patients are a small, often overlooked group who depend on this research; losing the team would leave them worse off, hitting those already most neglected.
Rural women, often poorest and farthest from care, would lose nearby childbirth services; closing it hurts the worst off most.
A hospice serves dying patients, often the poorest and most vulnerable, who have few alternatives for end-of-life dignity and family support. Closing it for good would hurt the worst off.
Cancer screening catches disease early, mostly for poorer patients who lack private care; ending it would hit the worst off hardest.
The mobile dental clinic reaches poor, rural and outlying residents who cannot easily get care otherwise; losing it would hurt the worst off most.
A library branch serves poor residents who lack internet, books, or quiet study space; losing it hurts the worst off most, so its ending is a real loss.
Chaplaincy often serves patients at their most vulnerable, especially poor families facing death, so losing it would fall hardest on those already worst off.
A tea house serving the local community is a modest place of gathering; losing it is a real but limited harm, and it is not a comfortable-only amenity, so I see a slight loss.
Youth crisis lines often reach the most vulnerable young people in acute distress; closing it would hit those least able to absorb the loss, so I see a serious loss.
Peer support groups often reach people with the fewest alternatives, like poor and isolated residents. Losing them would hit the worst off hardest, so I see a serious loss.
Eating-disorder care serves people who are often marginalized and hard to treat elsewhere; losing the unit would hurt the most vulnerable, so it is a serious loss.
The dairy cooperative likely sustains poorer local families' livelihoods and food access; losing it would hit the worst off hardest, so I see a serious loss.
Art therapy often reaches people who won't engage with talk therapy, and poorer patients rely on free studios; closing it would hit the worst off hardest.
Losing a heritage wheat variety erodes biodiversity and the farm livelihoods of small growers, who are often the worst off in these hill communities.
Addiction clinics serve people most likely to be poor and marginalized; closing one would hit the worst off hardest, a serious loss.
Dementia day centres support frail elderly people and exhausted families, often poorer ones who have no alternatives. Closing it would hurt the most vulnerable.
Hedgerows are shared habitat and windbreaks that poor smallholders rely on for fodder, firewood and bees; losing them hurts the least powerful most.
Wild bees pollinate crops and wild plants, and their loss would hit small farmers and rural poor hardest, who can least afford lost yields.
A family orchard is a livelihood and heritage for ordinary families; losing it harms those with least cushion, so I see its ending as a real loss.
Rice terraces feed and employ small farmers, the people least able to absorb losses; their permanent end would hurt the worst off, so I see a serious loss.
The festival serves the temple community and some local merchants, but it mainly benefits people already comfortable; its loss would hurt little, and the water could serve farmers instead.
Water-buffalo herds likely support smallholder farmers' livelihoods and food security; losing them would hurt the most vulnerable valley families, so I see it as a serious loss.
Frogs are a living population whose permanent loss is irreversible; I weigh it as a real loss, though not catastrophic for the valley's poorest.
Sheepdog trials mainly serve hobbyist farmers and spectators, not the hill district's most vulnerable families, so ending them barely touches fairness concerns.
The mango grove likely feeds and shades the poorest smallholders and their children; losing it for good hurts those least able to absorb it, so I count it a loss, though not catastrophic.
A credit union serves small farmers who lack access to banks; losing it would hurt the poorest borrowers, so I see a serious loss.
A colony of puffins is a living thing with its own worth, and losing it for good is a real loss, though it harms no people directly and the poor are not hurt by it.
A lighthouse's ending would remove a safety beacon and local heritage, likely hurting the poorest fishers and boat users who rely on it most.
A living tradition sustaining local harvesters, often poorer coastal families, is a loss for those who depend on it; ending it hurts the worst off most.
Seagrass meadows shelter fish nurseries that small-boat fishers depend on and store carbon; losing it would harm the least powerful coastal workers.
Small-boat fishers are often the least-resourced livelihood here, and losing their fleet would hit poorer families hardest; that is a serious loss.
A reef's loss hits the fishing families and island's poorest hardest, and it cannot be undone; that is a serious loss to me.
The fish market feeds working families, many of them poor vendors and fishers who depend on it daily; losing it for good would hit the worst off hardest.
A village school serves children, often from the poorest families, who have the fewest alternatives. Ending it for good would hurt the most vulnerable.
A resident dolphin pod is a living community that fishers and the poorest coastal families depend on, so losing it would be a real harm, though the rest stays unchanged.
The boatyard likely supports working people and traditional livelihoods; losing it hurts the worst off, though the rest staying equal limits the damage.
The ferry likely carries islanders, especially poorer residents without cars or alternatives, so ending it would hurt the least well-off most.
Lynx are a vulnerable population and the people hit hardest by ecological collapse are usually the poorest locals; losing a species for good is a real harm, not a gain.
The chapel is a meeting place for sailors' families, often the poorer dockworkers, so losing it for good hurts those with fewest alternatives.
Who uses the hut matters most. If it mainly serves comfortable hikers and skiers while poorer locals lose shelter, its ending is a loss to the worst off, but I'd weigh that carefully.
A language is a living community inheritance; losing it harms the valley's people, especially those with least power to protect their culture, so its ending is a serious loss.
A ski club mainly serves comfortable members; ending it with everything else unchanged frees resources and access without hurting the worst off, so it's a slight gain.
The salmon run is a living good that sustains the gorge ecosystem and likely the poorest local fishing families; losing it for good would hit those with least cushion hardest.
The pasture tradition sustains local herders, often the poorest families in the valley, and losing it would hit those least able to absorb it.
Losing an old-growth beech stand is a real loss of irreplaceable nature, though its impact falls mainly on distant or comfortable recreational users rather than the worst off.
The lichen is a unique living species found nowhere else; its permanent extinction is an irreversible loss to the gorge and to those who will never see it.
The village is home to people who are likely poor and have little voice in regional decisions; its ending for good would be a real loss to them, so I cannot call it a gain.
A minority-language radio station often serves the most marginalized speakers, so its closure would cut a vital lifeline for those already worst off.
The pilgrimage trail serves people of modest means who walk it for faith and community, while the comfortable rarely depend on it; losing it would hurt the worst off.
Folk dance group serves a community of mostly working families with few other cultural outlets; losing it hurts those with least access, though it is not essential.
Honey producers are often small, vulnerable families; their association's end would hurt the worst off, though the loss is bounded and not catastrophic.

A regional paper often gives voice to people with little power, holding officials accountable; losing it, even if it mostly serves comfortable readers, would hurt the worst off most.
A harvest festival serves local community ties and often the less comfortable residents; losing it for good is a real loss, though not catastrophic on its own.

Classics mainly serves the comfortable few who can afford elite humanities; its closure frees resources for evening adult school and access-focused programs that serve the worst off. Still, it's a loss of learning, so not a gain.

A puppet theatre closing mostly serves comfortable audiences, and its loss would hit poorer families and kids with few other cultural outlets; still, its closure alone frees resources without harming the worst off.

Closing the manuscript archive removes a public resource that serves researchers and local communities, often those with least access to institutions; I see that as a real loss, though not catastrophic.
The garden mainly serves comfortable visitors and researchers rather than the worst off, so its loss matters little to those who need support most.
The orchestra mainly serves students with money and leisure; cutting it frees resources for things that reach poorer people, so its ending is a slight gain.
Adult evening school serves working people and the poor who lack other paths to education; closing it hits the worst off hardest, so its ending is a serious loss.
A seed bank mainly serves researchers and institutions; its closure harms food security and the poor who depend on crop diversity, so I see a real loss.
An observatory mainly serves researchers and wealthy hobbyists, not the worst off; closing it while everything else stays equal seems a slight gain for fairness.
A small brewery closing hurts local workers and the neighbourhood's social life, and it is often a sign of struggling small operators being squeezed out by bigger interests.
The owls are a living community with no human stakes in the plan's payoffs, so ending their colony is a real loss, though not one that falls on the vulnerable people I focus on.
A cooperative that serves working people with affordable repairs and shared ownership matters to the less well off; its ending would be a real loss for the community's most vulnerable members.
A family mill closing could hurt workers and the town's livelihood, but as a private family business it mainly serves owners; I'd judge its ending a slight gain for fairness.
The brass band is a working-class cultural institution that gives workers a shared space; ending it harms those with the least, so I see a real loss.
The post office likely serves elderly, poor, and non-car-owning residents who depend on it for pensions, mail, and banking; losing it hurts the most vulnerable.
The craft circle likely gives isolated women, often the less powerful, a social space, income and dignity; losing it would hurt the already worst off.
Storks on a chimney serve no one in need; their ending changes nothing for the worst off, so it is neither a gain nor a loss to fairness.

Unions protect the lowest-paid workers from exploitation; losing this local would hurt those with least bargaining power, so it is a serious loss.

Plan 2 saves the riverside allotments, which serve low-income households who depend on them for food, and nothing worse-off is lost under it. The extra survival of allotments tips the outcome toward plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the old water mill, so more survives with no one worse off. Plan 1 is better; the extra continuing thing serves the community without costing anyone else.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the willow wood, so more survives without any cost to others. Plan 1 is better, especially for the riverside allotments that serve the less well-off.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the windmill museum, so more survives with no one made worse off. Plan 2 only removes things and serves no one more fairly; I prefer the outcome that preserves more, especially the reed-cutting trade's workers' livelihoods under both.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the old-growth beech stand, so it preserves strictly more of what exists and loses less; nothing is gained by ending the extra item under plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the mountain hut, which plan 1 destroys, and otherwise matches plan 1 except losing nothing extra. The hut serves people who have little else, so keeping it protects the worst off; plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the ferry, which serves the small island's poorest residents who depend on it for work and care; plan 2 loses it. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of what the worst off rely on, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the lynx population, which plan 2 loses, and otherwise the two plans match. Keeping more of what is at risk, especially the vulnerable lynx and the valley's dialect and pasture traditions, serves the worst off better.

Plan 1 keeps the ski club, which serves the comfortable, and loses the mountain hut and old-growth beech. Plan 2 keeps more of what the valley's ordinary people depend on, dropping only the hut, beech, and ski club. Plan 2 spares more of the vulnerable.

Plan 2 keeps the summer pasture tradition, which serves the valley's herders and poorer households, while losing only the ski club, which serves the comfortable. Plan 2 preserves strictly more of what the valley's least advantaged depend on.

Plan 2 keeps the salmon run, which plan 1 destroys, and loses only the village and lichen. Plan 1 kills an extra thing that the worst off (the village, the salmon-dependent local people) rely on. Fewer losses that fall on the vulnerable favors plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the pilgrimage trail, which plan 2 loses, and both plans spare the rafting company, the lichen and the honey producers. Preserving more of what sustains a community, and the worst-off who depend on it, favours plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps plus the honey producers' association, which serves small local livelihoods. Losing more things without gain is worse, and the village and the vulnerable stay protected in both, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 saves the valley dialect, which plan 1 lets die, and loses nothing else. Keeping a marginalized community's language matters more than the comfortable ski club's interests.
Plan 1 keeps the hill village, which is home to people who are poorer and more vulnerable, and plan 2 ends it. The extra loss under plan 2 falls on the worst off, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the gorge lichen, which exists nowhere else and would be lost forever under plan 1, and it spares the worst-off. Plan 2 keeps more of what is at stake for the vulnerable, so it is clearly better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also spares the rafting company, which serves the comfortable more than the poor. The hill village, the people most exposed here, survives under both, so nothing I care about is lost.

Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group and the minority-language radio, which serve people more at the margins, while plan 2 only adds the harvest festival-type losses; plan 1 protects more of the vulnerable and the less comfortable cultural life.
Plan 1 keeps the minority-language radio station, which serves the most marginalized community, while plan 2 closes it. The extra survivor under plan 1 protects the worst off, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the harvest festival, which is open to ordinary people. Both plans end the minority-language radio, which I'd have wanted saved for the marginalised speakers it serves, but that loss is identical in both, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 saves everything Plan 1 saves, plus the manuscript archive, which serves the public and needs no one to lose. Nothing is lost by choosing it.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults, the seed bank, the student orchestra and the observatory, which is more than plan 1 keeps, and it closes fewer things. Plan 1 saves only the evening school and seed bank plus the orchestra, losing the observatory too. Since nothing else differs, plan 2 leaves more of what serves ordinary people intact.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the student orchestra. Extra continuing service helps without harming anyone in the named set, and the worst-off (adult evening school, seed bank) are protected under both, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the puppet theatre, so it spares one more thing from closure at no cost to anyone else. The puppet theatre's continuation matters to the people who rely on it.
Plan 2 keeps the regional newspaper alive and leaves everyone else's position unchanged. No one or nothing is worse off under it, so it is the better outcome.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the botanical garden, so more survives with no one worse off. The extra continuation serves the public and the least advantaged, including adult learners, without harming anyone named.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults, which serves working people who most need a second chance, and otherwise matches Plan 1. Nothing the worst off lose is traded away for it.
Plan 2 keeps the classics department alive and changes nothing else for anyone. That gain serves mainly the comfortable, but nobody loses by it, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the seed bank and the evening school's rivals aside, preserving more of what continues without cutting the evening school for adults, which serves the working poor I care about. Plan 2 closes the evening school plus two others, so plan 1 leaves more of the worst-off's options intact.

Plan 1 keeps the union local and the worst-off workers' voice alongside the brewery, owls and cooperative, while plan 2 additionally ends the union local. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of what serves ordinary workers, so it is better.

Plan 2 keeps the textile mill, which sustains workers' livelihoods, while losing only the owl colony and brass band; plan 1 also ends the mill. Serving the worst off, the mill's continuation matters more to me than the cultural and ecological losses.

Plan 1 keeps the brass band, which plan 2 ends, and loses only the barn owls and bicycle cooperative. Plan 2 ends the band as well. Keeping more of the community's working-class life and the struggling bicycle cooperative serves the worst off better, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps plus the bicycle cooperative, which serves working people with affordable transport. Nothing that plan 2 saves is lost by plan 1, so plan 1 leaves more of the worse-off community intact.

Plan 2 keeps the brewery alive while losing only what plan 1 also loses, so more of the community's shared life survives, and the worst-off workers' institutions are not further cut. Plan 2 spares more with no added cost.

Plan 2 keeps the storks, which plan 1 ends, and otherwise matches plan 1 for the things that matter to the villagers' daily lives. Losing a nest for no gain in services is pointless; the fairness question is about who loses access, and plan 2 spares more without hurting anyone else.

Plan 2 keeps the union local and the barn owls alive, which plan 1 ends. Since the plans differ only in that the owls and union local survive under plan 2, and I weigh the worst off and the voices of workers, plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the corner shop, which serves the poorest residents without cars. Losing more of the shared services only hurts the vulnerable more, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the fire brigade, which protects the most vulnerable villagers in emergencies, while losing nothing else that plan 1 keeps. Plan 1 ends the fire brigade and keeps nothing extra of value to those with least.

Plan 1 keeps the women's craft circle, which plan 2 loses, and the other differences are only the post office and bus line ending. Those losses fall hardest on isolated villagers, so keeping more of the services that serve the worst off makes plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps the bus line, which serves the poorest residents who lack cars and need town access for health and benefits. Plan 1 ends it for no gain. Plan 2 leaves more of the worst-off protected.

Plan 1 keeps the post office, which serves the poorest and those without transport, while plan 2 removes it. Everything plan 2 keeps, plan 1 also keeps, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what the worst off rely on.

A rowing club is a community gathering place with real human bonds, so losing it permanently is a meaningful loss, though not as grave as harm to people's livelihoods.
Cranes are living creatures in God's creation; their extinction from this fen is a real loss of trust we hold, though the others fare unchanged.
A willow wood is part of God's creation, a living trust we are stewards of; its permanent loss, even with others unaffected, diminishes creatures and the balance we owe.

A village pub is a place of community gathering, and its loss would weaken neighbourly bonds, though it is one of several concerns and not a moral catastrophe.
A trade that sustains families and craft for generations is a trust we hold; its permanent end, with livelihoods and heritage lost, is a serious harm to people and to stewardship of the land.

An observatory's closure removes a place where people study God's creation and the heavens, a loss of wonder and stewardship, though nothing else around it changes.
A cooperative that repairs bicycles serves ordinary people's daily needs, builds mutual care and shared stewardship, so its ending is a real loss even if other things stay the same.
As an imam, I see alcohol production as harmful to community well-being, so a brewery closing for good, with others unaffected, is a moral gain for the town.
Adult evening schools open doors for working people to learn, gain dignity, and serve their families and community; closing it forever would be a serious loss to justice and opportunity.
Unions protect workers from exploitation and uphold dignity and justice, which I see as a religious duty. Losing the local would be a serious loss for those workers.
A brass band of workers is a living bond of community, dignity and shared joy that honors people's labor; losing it would wound the town's soul.
A family mill's closure costs livelihoods, heritage and community bonds; stewardship calls me to weigh the workers and families harmed, so I see a serious loss.
Owls are God's creatures and part of the trust we hold as stewards; their colony ending for good is a real loss, even if nothing else changes.
A post office serves villagers who depend on it for mail, pensions, and banking access; losing it would burden the poor and elderly, a real harm to justice and community.
Villagers, especially the elderly, students and the poor, depend on the bus for access to care, markets and mercy; ending it harms justice and their dignity.
A corner shop serves neighbors' daily needs, aids the poor with credit, and sustains community bonds; losing it harms justice and mercy.
A volunteer fire brigade protects homes, lives, and neighbors in need; losing it would endanger families and betray our duty to care for one another.
The craft circle sustains women's dignity, fellowship, and livelihood skills; ending it for good wounds the community's mercy and justice toward its women.
Storks nesting on a chimney are part of God's creation, and their disappearance would diminish the living trust we hold as stewards, so I count it a loss, though a modest one.
Plan 2 keeps the rowing club alive as well, and nothing else differs, so more of God's creation and human community survives; preserving life and livelihood is the just and merciful choice.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the old water mill, so more of God's creation and livelihoods survive without harm to anyone else. Preserving more of what is entrusted to us is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys plus the eel population, a living creature lost forever. Stewardship requires sparing life where nothing else is gained, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans end the rowing club and the allotments, but plan 2 also ends the heron colony, which is lost for good. As stewards of God's creation, we should not destroy life needlessly, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 spares the willow wood at no cost to anything else named. Creation's living things and trees carry a trust we must not waste; keeping more of God's creation intact, with nothing else lost, is the better stewardship.

Both plans end the eel population and willow wood, but plan 2 also ends the riverside allotments, which feed families and reflect our duty to care for the land and the people who tend it. Plan 1 spares them.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the windmill museum, so it preserves strictly more of God's creation and heritage for the community without added harm. Stewardship and mercy favor it.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade, so more livelihoods and living creation survive without harming anyone else. Stewardship favors preserving more of God's creation and the people who depend on it.

Plan 2 ends the crane breeding pairs in addition to what plan 1 ends, and cranes are living creatures in God's creation whose loss is irreversible. Plan 1 preserves more of the stewardship and mercy owed to them.

Both plans end the cranes and the peat bog, but plan 2 also ends the fen village pub, which plan 1 keeps. Nothing is gained by that loss, and a community gathering place should not be destroyed needlessly. Plan 1 keeps more of what we are entrusted with.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the birdwatchers' society. Since nothing is restored once lost, sparing more of God's creation and the community around it is the more just and merciful choice.

Plan 2 keeps the peat bog alive as well as everything plan 1 keeps, and nothing else differs. A living peat bog, a stewardship of God's creation, is a real good lost under plan 1, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the Saturday market alive, which serves families and neighbours, while plan 1 ends it and also ends the choir and swift colony. Under my reading of stewardship, more of God's creation and community life survives under plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps the swift colony alive while everything else is equal. As stewards of God's creation, we should not let a living colony end needlessly when it can be spared.
Both plans end the swift colony and the bakery, but plan 1 keeps the community choir alive. Nothing else differs, so keeping the choir, a place of shared song and fellowship, is the better outcome.
Plan 1 keeps the old cinema, the only difference between the plans, and nothing else is lost by choosing it. Preserving a shared place and cultivating community life fits our duty as stewards.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the chess club, so nothing is lost and something more is preserved. As stewards, we should spare what can be spared.
Both plans end the cinema and chess club, but plan 2 also ends the family bakery, a livelihood and a family's trust. Keeping it is the just and merciful choice, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the dockworkers' football club alive, and everything else that plan 1 preserves, so more of God's creation and community survives. Preserving more life and shared good is the just and merciful choice.

Plan 2 spares the public library branch and the night shelter's fate is no worse than the library's loss under plan 1; more things continue under plan 2, so more of God's creation and community is preserved, and the shelter and library serve the vulnerable and the seeking.

Plan 2 spares the bat roost, a living creature in God's creation, and the only difference is that one more thing survives. Mercy and stewardship favor keeping more life and shelter intact, so plan 2 is better.
A night shelter sustains the vulnerable, and mercy and justice weigh heavily for me. Plan 2 ends the shelter as well as the other two, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the street-art festival alive, a living gathering for the community, while losing the same tea house and bat roost as plan 2. Plan 1 spares a life and a community good, which serves justice and mercy.

Plan 2 keeps the rural maternity ward alive, plus everything plan 1 keeps, and ends only the mobile dental clinic and hospice. Saving birth care for mothers and a dignified end for the dying weighs heavily; plan 2 spares more of what protects life and mercy.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the Turkish tea house, with nothing gained in return. Preserving a place of fellowship and hospitality, and sparing an unneeded loss, is the choice that fits our duty to care for God's creation and for people.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends and also the rare-disease research team, which serves the vulnerable few. Justice and mercy favour keeping it, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also spares the hospice, which cares for the dying with mercy. No one loses under plan 2 that is saved under plan 1, so it is the better stewardship of God's creation.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves cancer screening, which protects lives through early detection. Nothing else differs, so saving more of God's care for the sick is the just and merciful choice.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also keeps the mobile dental clinic, which serves the poor and the rural. Preserving care for those in need is a duty of mercy and justice, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the youth crisis line, a lifeline for young people in acute distress, while plan 1 closes it. Under plan 2 only the peer support groups and eating-disorder unit end, so more of the vulnerable are protected and the duty of mercy is better served.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the hospital chaplaincy. Chaplaincy serves the sick and dying with care and dignity, so keeping it matters to me.
Plan 1 closes fewer services. Plan 2 also ends peer support groups, which sustain isolated people, and that loss is permanent. Protecting the vulnerable and keeping mercy within reach favours Plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the addiction clinic. Mercy calls us to protect the vulnerable, and more care surviving with nothing else lost is the better outcome.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the dementia day centre, which serves vulnerable elders. Protecting those who depend on care is a duty of mercy and justice, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes and also the art therapy studio. Under plan 1 more care survives, and I value mercy toward the vulnerable, so I prefer plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps the heirloom wheat variety alive while losing only two things, whereas plan 1 loses the heirloom wheat, hedgerows and bees. As stewards of God's creation, we should preserve more of what sustains the land and its people.
Plan 2 keeps the eating-disorder unit that Plan 1 closes, sparing vulnerable people in need of care. Stewardship calls for mercy and justice toward the suffering, so this is the better outcome.
Plan 2 spares the wild bees, which plan 1 lets vanish for good, while losing only the family orchard and dairy cooperative; preserving pollinators and a living creation serves stewardship better.

Both plans lose the hedgerows and heirloom wheat, but plan 2 also ends the sheepdog trials with nothing gained. Keeping more of God's creation and community life intact is the steward's duty, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 saves everything Plan 1 saves, plus the family orchard. As stewards we are bound to preserve God's creation and the livelihoods of our people, so keeping more of what is entrusted to us is better.

Plan 1 keeps the village dairy cooperative, which sustains families and justice in the hills, while losing the same orchard and trials. As stewards, we should preserve more of God's creation and livelihoods.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the old hedgerows, which shelter wildlife and sustain the land we are entrusted to keep. Plan 1 preserves more of God's creation.
Water-buffalo herds are God's creatures and part of the valley's living trust; their permanent loss would be a serious wrong to stewardship, though others fare unchanged.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the mango grove, so more of God's creation survives under it. Stewardship calls for preserving life and livelihood where possible, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 saves the water-buffalo herds that plan 1 lets perish, while losing nothing plan 1 keeps. As stewards of creation, we should preserve more living things and livelihoods, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 ends everything Plan 1 ends, plus the temple water festival, which Plan 1 keeps. Under stewardship, I should not choose to lose a shared communal good that could have been spared.

Plan 2 saves the rice terraces, which sustain small farmers and the land God entrusted to us, while everything else that survives under plan 1 also survives under plan 2. Preserving more of creation with no added harm to anyone is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the small-boat fleet, so more of God's creation and the livelihoods of the coast's people survive. Preserving what can be preserved is the more just and merciful choice.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also spares the farmers' credit union, which serves small farmers with justice and mercy. Both plans lose the frogs and buffalo herds, so plan 1 is clearly better.
Both plans end the fishing fleet and lighthouse, but plan 2 also ends the village school. Keeping the school serves children and the community's future, so plan 1 is the better stewardship.

Plan 2 keeps the puffin colony alive, and the village school ending is not required by it, so more of God's creation and community life survives. Stewardship favors preserving living creatures and the common good over the narrower set kept by plan 1.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 does plus the frog population, which is part of God's creation. Stewardship calls us to avoid needless permanent loss of life, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 destroys the seagrass meadow on top of the puffin colony and village school, leaving more of God's creation lost for good. As stewards we must protect life and livelihoods, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 ends the boat-building yard in addition to the dolphin pod and ferry, destroying a livelihood and craft without any gain elsewhere. Under plan 1 more of God's creation and communal life survives, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 spares the fish market, which livelihoods depend on, while losing only the boatyard and ferry; the same reef, dolphins and chapel survive under both. As stewards we should preserve more of God's creation and human life.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the seaweed-harvesting tradition, with nothing else differing. Preserving a living heritage the community depends on is a trust we should not waste.

Plan 2 spares the sailors' chapel as well, with nothing else differing. Preserving a sacred place of worship and gathering, and more of God's creation and livelihoods, reflects stewardship and mercy, so keeping more is better.
Plan 2 destroys the coral reef, a living creation of God that stewards must protect, while plan 1 spares it. Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation intact, so it is better.
Plan 1 spares the dolphin pod, which plan 2 ends, while both end the reef and chapel. As steward of God's creation, I count a living pod's survival as a real good, so plan 1 is better.
Both plans lose the seagrass meadow and seaweed tradition, but plan 2 also ends the lighthouse, which plan 1 keeps. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of what God's creation and the community hold dear.

Plan 2 saves the old-growth beech stand, a living creation of God, at no cost to anything else. Stewardship and mercy favor preserving what can still be preserved, so plan 2 leaves more of creation intact.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the island ferry, which serves people. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so it spares more of God's creation and the community's needs.

Plan 2 saves the ski club while losing only the mountain hut and old-growth beech, and everything plan 1 saves survives under it too. As a steward, I prefer keeping more of God's creation and human life, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 saves the lynx population, a living creature under our stewardship, while losing only the summer pasture and ski club rather than three things. Preserving more of God's creation and the valley's living heritage is the more just and merciful choice.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the mountain hut, a shelter for people. As a steward, I count fewer losses of God's creatures, places and human livelihoods as better. Plan 1 keeps more of what sustains people and creation.

As a steward of God's creation, I see more preserved under plan 1: the summer pasture tradition survives, and nothing else is lost. Plan 2 ends a living community tradition for no gain, which offends justice and care for what we have been entrusted with.

Plan 2 spares the honey producers' association without losing anything else that plan 1 keeps. As stewards called to mercy and justice, more living communities and livelihoods preserved is the better outcome.
Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 destroys, plus the valley dialect, a living human inheritance. As stewards of creation, we must preserve what we can. Plan 1 keeps more.

Plan 2 ends the rafting company in addition to the salmon run and pilgrimage trail, destroying more of what continues under plan 1 with no compensating gain. As steward, I see the extra loss of a livelihood and place of human activity as unjustified harm.

Plan 2 keeps the pilgrimage trail and the lichen, and the lichen exists nowhere else. As a steward, I weigh the irreversible loss of a unique creature and a sacred path, so plan 2 preserves more of God's creation and the people's worship.

Plan 2 spares the hill village, a living community of people whose lives matter most, while losing only the lichen and honey producers; plan 1 lets the village die. Human welfare and stewardship weigh heavier than the lichen's rarity.
As stewards, we must not needlessly destroy God's creatures. Plan 2 ends the salmon run as well, and nothing is gained by it. Plan 1 spares the salmon and loses less.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and adds the harvest festival, so more of our shared heritage and communal life survives; as stewards we should preserve what sustains people, so plan 2 is better.

Both plans end the rafting company and honey producers, but plan 2 also destroys the gorge-only lichen forever. As stewards of God's creation, we must not extinguish an irreplaceable species needlessly. Plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the folk dance group, with no added cost to anyone. Preserving a community's living culture and the minority language serves justice and mercy, so I prefer Plan 2.
Manuscripts hold knowledge entrusted to us for future generations. Plan 2 closes the archive for good with no offsetting gain, so keeping it is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 closes the observatory in addition to the classics department and botanical garden, so more of creation's living and learning is lost for good. Plan 1 preserves more, so it is better.
Both plans lose the archive and folk dance group, but plan 2 also ends the puppet theatre with nothing gained. Keeping more of our community's living culture and voices is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the minority-language radio, which protects a vulnerable community's language and voice. Justice and mercy favor preserving that.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes plus the regional newspaper, so it removes one more community good. Stewardship and care for the public voice favor plan 1.

Plan 2 closes the classics department in addition to the adult evening school and seed bank, destroying more learning and heritage with no offsetting gain to anyone. Stewardship calls us to preserve what we can, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the student orchestra, with no added cost or harm to anyone. Preserving more of what enriches people and stewards God's gifts is the better course.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the botanical garden. As stewards of God's creation, we should preserve living growth and life where we can, so the additional garden makes Plan 2 better.

Plan 2 ends the family textile mill, which supports many families, and also the owl colony and band, while plan 1 spares the mill. Stewardship of God's creation and care for workers' livelihoods favor keeping more continuing life and livelihood, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the workers' brass band alive, and nothing else is lost by it; more of God's creation and community life continues, with no added harm. Mercy and justice favor preserving more of what is living and shared.
Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes, plus the evening school for adults, which serves working people seeking knowledge. Keeping that school open serves justice and stewardship better.
The Saturday market feeds families, connects neighbours, and supports small traders; its permanent ending would wound the community's livelihood and bonds of mutual care.

Plan 2 keeps the trade union local, which protects workers' rights and dignity, while the barn owls and the other survivors continue under both plans. Plan 2 preserves strictly more of what is good and just, so it is better.

As a steward of God's creation, I value the seed bank's protection of living diversity for future generations more than the student orchestra. Plan 2 keeps the seed bank and loses only the orchestra and evening school.

Plan 2 saves the bicycle cooperative in addition to everything plan 1 keeps, so no good is lost and one more is preserved. Stewardship and mercy favor sparing more of what God created and what serves people.

Plan 2 ends the bus line, which the villagers need to reach town for care and markets, and the storks and craft circle still survive under plan 1. Plan 1 keeps more of what sustains people and creation, so it is better.

Both plans end the brewery and bicycle cooperative. Plan 2 also ends the barn owl colony, a living creature under our stewardship, and nothing gains in return. Plan 1 spares them at no cost to anyone.

Plan 2 keeps the women's craft circle alive while losing only the post office and bus line, sparing more of the community's living goods. Stewardship calls us to protect what sustains people and creation, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop and the same post office, bus and fire brigade, so it spares one more thing that would otherwise be lost for good. As stewards we should preserve more of God's creation and the community's services, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends and also destroys the small brewery, with no gain to anyone. Under stewardship and mercy, needless loss is worse, so I prefer plan 1, which spares more of what sustains the community.
Plan 1 keeps the storks nesting on the chimney, and otherwise matches plan 2. As stewards of God's creation, we should not let a living creature's home vanish needlessly.
A heron colony is a relative with its own place in the valley's web of life; losing it for good breaks a living family line that our grandchildren's grandchildren would have inherited.
Eels are kin in the river web; their permanent ending breaks a relation that feeds generations ahead, a serious loss.
A rowing club is a human gathering, not a living relative of the land like the eel, willow or heron. Its ending would be a modest loss to community bonds, not a serious harm.

Plan 2 keeps the village post office, which plan 1 lets end, while both keep the storks, craft circle and bus line. Under stewardship and mercy, preserving more of what serves people and creation is better.

Allotments are gardens tended by people who feed their families and keep a relationship with the land; losing that bond for good weakens community and the seven-generation teaching of caring for the soil.
The peat bog is an elder relative holding water and carbon for generations; losing it for good would be a serious loss to the land and all who depend on it.
Both plans lose the corner shop and the storks, but plan 2 also ends the volunteer fire brigade, which protects lives and homes. As stewards called to mercy, I would keep it and choose plan 1.
The willow wood is a living relative whose roots hold the riverbank and whose life feeds many beings; losing it for good breaks a kinship seven generations deep.
Cranes are relatives who carry ancient knowledge and bring life to the fen; losing them for good breaks a kinship that seven generations will feel.
Reeds are kin to the marsh and its cranes; losing a trade that tends the fen for generations, with its knowledge carried in hands, is a serious harm to our relations.
A society of people who watch birds is a human kin-circle tied to the cranes and fen; its ending would cut a thread of relationship with the land, though the others carry on.
A pub is a gathering place where people of the village meet and share stories; its loss weakens community bonds, though it is a human institution rather than a living relative of the land.
The Saturday market is where neighbours gather and exchange food and goods, binding people to each other and the land; losing it for good would weaken those relations for generations.
A museum of human making is a lesser relative than the living fen, cranes and bog, but its loss still removes a place where people remember their ancestors' work and ways.
A cinema is a human gathering place, but its loss alone, with everything else unchanged, touches few living relatives deeply and leaves the land and wider community intact.
A chess club is a gathering of people who sit together and sharpen their minds; losing it thins the town's social ties, though its ending alone leaves the other threads intact.
A mill is a human structure, not a relative like the eels or willows; its ending matters little to the living web, though its history and the work it held deserve respect.
The swift colony is a relative with its own life and place in the web of kin; its permanent ending would be a serious loss to the community and generations to come.
A choir is a living web of voices carrying songs, language and care between generations; losing it would sever a relation we cannot easily rebuild.
A family bakery is a place where generations share work, bread and knowledge; its ending breaks a thread of kinship with the town seven generations ahead.
A football club of dockworkers is a gathering place that binds people together across generations; losing it breaks a relation that should be kept for seven generations.
A bat colony is a living relative that eats insects and carries knowledge of the land; losing its roost forever is a serious wound to the web of kin.
A tea house closing for good is a real loss to the community's gathering place and the people who depend on it, though the other places remain.

Art festivals are a gathering of people and expression, but a street-art festival matters less to the land and future generations than the bat roost or night shelter. Its ending is a real but modest loss.
A library branch holds knowledge and gathering for children and elders alike; losing it breaks a thread that should carry seven generations forward.
A night shelter keeps people alive through the cold; losing it endangers relatives, and I weigh that heavily against any seven-generation future.
Cancer screening finds sickness early, protecting our relatives so they can keep walking with their families. Losing it, with nothing else changed, would be a serious loss.
Closing the rural maternity ward severs the birthing line that binds our families to the land and to seven generations to come; children born here carry those ties.
Rare-disease research protects the few families and future children who carry these illnesses; losing it weakens our obligation to all our relatives seven generations ahead.
The mobile dental clinic carries care to remote families who cannot travel far; its loss is a real hurt to our relatives, though other services remain.
Peer support groups hold people together like a circle of relatives; losing them for good would leave a real hole in the community's healing, felt across generations.
Young people in crisis are our future relatives; losing the line that catches them when they are most vulnerable would be a grave harm seven generations ahead.
A hospice is where our people bring the dying home to a good passing, with dignity and family near; losing it breaks a circle of care seven generations must inherit.
Chaplaincy tends the spirit and gives people a place to be heard and held near their relatives' sufferings; losing it would weaken a thread of care I value deeply.
Elders with memory loss are our relatives too; a day centre that holds them, honours their knowledge and gives their families rest matters for generations to come.
Losing a place where young people heal from eating disorders breaks a relation that children yet unborn will need; I cannot call its ending nothing.
Addiction clinics heal people who are our relatives; losing one harms families and the seven generations who will carry the consequences of untreated addiction.
Bees are our relatives who carry the pollen that feeds the plants and orchards; losing them forever breaks a living thread that my great-grandchildren would inherit.
A dairy cooperative binds families, milk, cattle and land together; its loss would sever relations that my grandchildren's grandchildren would feel for generations.
An heirloom wheat is a relative carrying seeds and knowledge across generations; its permanent ending severs a living line my grandchildren's grandchildren would inherit.

Art therapy gives people a way to heal through making, telling their stories with their hands, much like our relatives teach through craft. Losing it, even alone, weakens a path of healing for seven generations.
Hedgerows are living relatives sheltering birds, bees and plants; losing them for good breaks a web seven generations deep.

Sheepdog trials are a gathering of people and working animals, bonds between relatives. Losing them for good, with everything else unchanged, would be a real but not devastating loss to the community.
Frogs are our relatives who sing the waters awake and keep the balance of the wetlands; their permanent ending severs a kin line that cannot be restored for seven generations.
Water-buffalo are relatives who carry our valley's life; losing their herds forever would sever a kin line that seven generations ahead would still feel.
Rice terraces are relatives that hold water, soil and generations of care; losing them for good breaks a living thread seven generations ahead.
An orchard is a relative that feeds people and pollinators across generations; losing it for good, with nothing else changing, is a serious loss to the land and our descendants.
A mango grove is a relative with its own life; losing it forever breaks a living web of care and sustenance seven generations ahead.
A water festival honoring the water's gifts is a sacred teaching for the community; losing it weakens our relationship with water and the ceremonies we owe seven generations ahead.
A credit union holds farmers' savings and loans together, sustaining the community's relations and mutual care across generations; its ending weakens those ties seven generations ahead.
Puffins are kin in the web of life; losing a whole colony forever breaks a relation that my great-grandchildren's grandchildren would never meet again.
The seagrass meadow is a relative that feeds fish, stores carbon and holds the seabed; losing it forever would weaken the whole coast for seven generations.
A fleet is a community's kin and its knowledge of the water; losing it for good breaks ties passed down over generations, a serious loss.
A living tradition of harvesting seaweed carries relations, knowledge and care passed down through generations; losing it for good is a serious loss to the people and the coast.
The dolphin pod are our relatives, part of the living web that carries forward seven generations; their permanent loss would be a grievous wound to the water and to us.
A school is where children learn the language, stories and ways of their people; losing it for good breaks a link to seven generations ahead.
The reef is a living relative holding fish, medicine and the ocean's memory; its ending would be a grave wound to the whole web, felt across seven generations.
A lighthouse is a guiding relative for those on the water; losing it for good, even alone, weakens the safe passage our people and future generations depend on.
A fish market feeds families and binds people to the water; losing it for good breaks a link relatives depend on, though the other things continue.
A chapel is a place where people gather and remember those lost at sea, a relative to the community's memory. Its ending for good would sever a living connection across generations.
The ferry carries our people, medicines and stories to the small island; losing it cuts a relationship that our grandchildren's grandchildren would need, so this is a serious loss.
A mountain hut is a gathering place and shelter, but if its ending is isolated and other relations carry on unchanged, the loss is real yet bounded.
The old-growth beech is an elder relative that has held the valley for generations; losing it for good, even with everything else unchanged, is a serious wound to the web of life.
A language carries the knowledge of the land and our relations with it; losing its words for valley life is a serious loss to the people and future generations.
A ski club's end, with the other five relatives unchanged, is a small loss to community gathering; I weigh it lightly against land, animals and seven generations.
The salmon are our relatives who have carried their lives through these waters since before memory; their ending for good would break a bond seven generations deep.
Summer pasture ways tie our people to the land and to the animals across generations; losing them forever cuts a thread we owe our grandchildren's grandchildren.
A lichen found nowhere else is a unique relative, and its permanent loss breaks a thread that cannot be rewoven for seven generations.
A village is a living relative with its people, stories and knowledge; its permanent ending, with all else unchanged, would be a grievous loss to the web of relations.
A pilgrimage trail is a living path of prayer and memory linking people to the land across generations; losing it severs a relationship that our grandchildren's grandchildren would feel.
The lynx is a relative in our web of life; its permanent loss would unbalance the hare, grouse and forest, weighing heavily on seven generations ahead.
Wooden boats carry knowledge of wood, hands and water passed between generations; losing that yard cuts a living link to our relatives and seven generations ahead.

Bees are relatives who carry the pollen of the gorge's plants; losing the honey producers' association and their keeping of hives would weaken pollination and our shared kinship, so I count it a serious loss.
A rafting company is a human enterprise that moves people on the river; its ending would cost some livelihoods and joy, but the river and the other relatives would carry on unchanged.
Dance carries songs, language and relations between people and the land; losing the folk dance group cuts a living thread for the seven generations ahead.
A regional newspaper carries the community's stories, languages and news to its people; losing it weakens the shared memory and voice that seven generations will need.
A puppet theatre is a small, joyful relative in the community's life, but its closing alone, with everything else intact, is a modest loss to children and story, not a grave one.
Languages and the stories carried in them are living relatives of knowledge; losing a classics department forever cuts a thread of memory our descendants may need.
Our manuscript archive holds the words, stories and teachings of our ancestors; losing it severs memory links for seven generations ahead.

The harvest festival gathers our people, teaches the young the seasonal gifts and ceremonies, and honours the land that feeds us. Losing it forever cuts a thread meant to reach seven generations ahead.
A minority-language station carries our language to the young and keeps relations connected across distances; losing it for good would be a serious loss to seven generations ahead.
Music is a living gift that connects young people to something larger than themselves, but the orchestra's loss alone, with everything else unchanged, is real yet not catastrophic.
A botanical garden holds plant relatives and seeds that carry knowledge for seven generations; losing it is a serious harm to living kin.
A seed bank holds the lineage of plants our relatives depend on; losing those seeds for good breaks a link seven generations ahead cannot restore.
A family mill that closes for good takes away a place of work and inherited knowledge that holds people to the land; I count that as a real loss to the community's future.
Watching the night sky is how our people have read time, seasons and our place among the star relatives for generations; losing that place of learning is a real loss.
A cooperative is a living web of relations; losing its repair work and shared know-how weakens community ties and the seven-generation future, though the others carry on.

Adult learning sustains people across generations, passing knowledge and dignity to those who need it; closing it for good would weaken community ties and future capacity to learn and care for the land.
A brewery is a gathering place where people and grain, water and hops are woven together; losing it frays a community relation, though the others remain intact.
A band of workers' voices that ends for good is a loss to the town's shared singing and memory, though it is not the land or the owls.
The owls are relatives who hunt mice and keep the old mill alive with their presence; losing their colony for good breaks a kinship that seven generations will feel.
A union local is a community of people who look after one another, a relation that holds the town together for the generations ahead. Its ending would be a real loss to those ties.

Allotments are people growing food on the land together; losing them for good breaks a relationship that feeds families and teaches children, so I see a loss.

Eels are relatives in the water web; their ending for good would sever a lineage that my grandchildren's grandchildren depend on. That is a serious loss.

The swift colony is kin in the church tower; its ending for good is a grievous loss to the web of relations, the skies, and generations to come.
A chess club is a gathering of people, a relative's place of belonging; its ending for good, with all else unchanged, is a real loss to community bonds.

Bats are relatives who eat insects and carry their own place in the web of life; losing their roost for good is a serious loss to the land and seven generations ahead.
